title: N は N です。 <noun-predicate sentence>
body_lines: 「は」 is the “topic particle” in noun-predicate sentences, used to mark the subject/topic of the sentence; it is read “wa”.
Because 「は」 marks the topic, it usually has no direct English translation.

The sentence-final 「です」 is the “copula”, equivalent to “am/is/are”, much like the verb “be” in English. At the same time, ending a sentence with 「です」 also conveys the speaker's polite tone toward the listener.
① 私は山田です。／I'm Yamada.
② 李さんは中国人です。／Li is Chinese.
③ 中村さんは日本人です。／Nakamura is Japanese.
source_file: 初级上/1.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第5课.md

title: N は N ではありません。 <negative form of the noun-predicate sentence>
category: negative form of the noun-predicate sentence
body_lines: 「ではありません」 is the negative form of 「です」, equivalent to “is not”. The 「では
in 「ではありません」 is mostly used in formal settings such as speeches or in writing; its colloquial form is
「じゃ」。
① 私は学生ではありません。／I am not a student.
② 佐藤さんは会社員ではありません。／Sato is not a company employee.
③ ジョージさんはイギリス人じゃありません。／George is not British.
This lesson focused on the expressions of noun-predicate sentences in the polite non-past tense. Summarized in the ta-
Table 5-1: Conjugation table of noun-predicate sentences in the polite non-past tense
Tense | Affirmative | Negative
Present/Future | 学生です。 | 学生ではありません。
Past | 学生でした。 | 学生ではありませんでした。
(In spoken language, 「では」 can be replaced by 「じゃ」)
source_file: 初级上/1.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第5课.md

title: Sentence + か。 <question>
body_lines: The particle 「か」 attached to the end of a declarative sentence forms a question, like the question mark in English. In writing,
Japanese questions generally do not use “?” but end with “。” instead. 「か」 can be attached to a declarative sentence
to form a yes-no question; such sentences are usually answered with 「はい」 or 「いいえ」.
A question word can also be added to form a wh-question; the respondent answers directly according to the meaning of the question word.
When 「か」 marks a question, the sentence is read with rising intonation.
① A: （あなたは）山田さんですか。／Are you Yamada?
B: はい、そうです。／Yes, I am.
② A: 山田さんは学生ですか。／Yamada, are you a student?
B: いいえ、（私は）学生じゃありません。／No, I'm not a student.
③ A: 経済学部の先生はどなたですか。／Who is the teacher in the economics department?
B: あの方です。／It's that person over there.
Adding 「か」 to a declarative sentence can also express confirmation; in this case the sentence is read with falling intonation.
① A: あのう、李由加です。／Um..., I'm Li Yuka.
B: あ、李さんですか。／Ah, it's Li.
② A：あの方は社員じゃありません。社長です。／That person is not a staff member. He's
the company president.
B: 社長ですか。／The president, I see.
② A：ジョージさんはアメリカ人で、経済学部の三年生です。／George is Ameri-
can, and a third-year student in the economics department.
B: そうですか。／I see.
source_file: 初级上/1.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第5课.md

title: N で、N です。 <noun conjunction (continuative form)>
body_lines: “で” is the continuative form of “です”, used to connect noun sentences. In this lesson, when two noun-predicate
sentences share the same subject, they can be joined into one sentence with “で”, and the subject of the second clause can be omitted. Here,
the two clauses are in a sequential relationship. Between Japanese clauses, the comma “、” is generally used
rather than “，”.
① ジョージさんはアメリカ人で、 留学生です。／George is American, and an international
student.
② こちらは中村さんで、日本人です。／This is Nakamura, who is Japanese.
③ あの方はイタリア人で、デザイナーです。／He/She is Italian, and a design-
er.
source_file: 初级上/1.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第5课.md

title: N の N <possession>
body_lines: The particle “の” placed between two nouns indicates possession or an attributive relation, like “'s” or “of” in English.
① ジョージさんは経済学部の学生です。／George is a student in the economics department.
② 由加：あの方は中村さんの先生ですか。／Is that person your teacher, Nakamura?
中村：はい、そうです。私の先生です。／Yes, that's right. He's my teacher.
③ 李さんは大学院の一年生です。／Li is a first-year graduate student.
source_file: 初级上/1.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第5课.md

title: Sentence + ね。 <confirmation (sentence-final particle ね-1)>
body_lines: The particle “ね” attached to the end of a sentence expresses the tone of “seeking confirmation” from the listener. It is one of the more
commonly used “sentence-final particles” in Japanese — particles used at the end of a sentence. When “ね” expresses “confirmation”,
it is read with rising intonation and a crisp feel.
① こんにちは。中村さんですね。／Hello. You're Nakamura, right?
② A: 紹介します。こちらは佐藤さんです。／Let me introduce you. This
is Sato.
B: 初めまして。佐藤さんですね。／Nice to meet you. You're Sato, right?
source_file: 初级上/1.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第5课.md

title: Subjects in Japanese
body_lines: Compared with Chinese or English, Japanese usually omits subjects such as “I”, “you”, and “he/she”. For ex-
example:
A: Are you Yamada?
B: Yes, I'm Yamada.
In Japanese, this would more often be expressed as:
（◯）A: 山田さんですか。
B: はい、山田です。
It would generally not be said this way:
（△）A: あなたは山田さんですか。
B: はい、私は山田です。
Japanese also rarely uses the second person “あなた” (you). If you must refer to “you”,
people generally address the other person directly by name, adding “さん”, or use their title such as “先
生” or “社長”, as a sign of respect. For example:
（△）これはあなたのですか。／Is this yours?
（◯）これは中村さんのですか。／Is this yours, Nakamura?
When addressing others, regardless of their gender or age, you can add “さん” after their name to show
respect, e.g. “中村さん”, “ジョージさん”. But when introducing your own name, you must not
add “さん” to your own name.
① 由加：あのう、李由加です。／I'm Li Yuka.
中村：あ、李さんですか。初めまして。中村絵里です。こんにちは。
／Ah, is it Li? Nice to meet you. I'm Nakamura Eri. Hello.
由加：こんにちは。中村さんですね。／Hello. You're Nakamura, right?
In addition, third-person words such as “彼” and “彼女” are not often used either. Although “彼” means “he”,
it can also mean “boyfriend”; although “彼女” means “she”, it can also mean “girlfriend”.
So how should you express “he/she”? Generally, you can add “さん” after the person's name,
such as “李さん”, “中村さん”. If you don't know the person's name, you can also use “あの方”
for the third person, or use the person's title directly, such as “先生”, “社長”, instead of “彼”
“彼女” — and this is more polite.
② A: あの方はどなたですか。／Who is that person?
B:（あの方は）佐藤さんです。／(He) is Sato.
source_file: 初级上/1.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第5课.md

title: Useful expressions for first meetings in this lesson
body_lines: (1) When you take the initiative to approach and speak to someone
When you take the initiative to approach someone, you can use “あのう” followed by what you want to say.
“あのう” is a filler word Japanese people often use, equivalent to “um...”. When talking with strang-
ers, you can start with “あのう” to avoid sounding abrupt. But it is not recommended to overuse it, or you will
sound long-winded.
① A: あのう、中国の方ですか。／Excuse me, are you Chinese?
B: はい、そうです。／Yes, that's right.
② A: あのう…／Um...
B: はい、何ですか。／Yes, what is it?
(2) The “three-step self-introduction” for first meetings
When meeting someone for the first time, you should first introduce yourself. A simple self-introduction in Japanese
can follow this order:
Step 1: greeting
Step 2: introduce who you are
Step 3: exchange pleasantries
Step 1: greeting
A self-introduction is usually given to someone you don't know, or in fairly formal settings,
so for the greeting part you can choose “おはようございます”,
“こんにちは”, or “こんばんは” depending on the time of day.
In addition, add “初めまして”. “初めまして” is the greeting for a first meeting, with the
meaning “nice to meet you (please treat me well)”.
Step 2: introduce who you are
When introducing yourself to others, note that you must not add the honorific “さん” or titles such as “社
長” or “部長” to yourself. You can use the following sentences to introduce yourself; sentence ② is more po-
lite and humble than ①.
① （私は）〇〇です。／I'm ____.
② （私は）〇〇と申します。／My name is ____. (humble)
You can also briefly introduce basic facts about yourself as appropriate, such as nationality, age, etc. For example:
③ （私は）経済学部の新入生です。／I'm a new student in the economics department.
④ （私は）中国から来ました。／I come from China.
The particle “から” means “from”. “来ました” means “came”; “ました”
follows a verb to form its past tense. This sentence means “I came from China”. Here too,
the subject “私は” is omitted.
Step 3: exchange pleasantries
Finally, as a closing, add “please treat me well”. All three of the following mean “please treat me well”,
but with slightly different tones: in general you can use ②; if great politeness is not needed,
use ①; for very formal occasions requiring a very polite tone, use ③. When the other person asks you to treat them well,
you can reply with ④.
① （どうぞ、）よろしく。／Please treat me well.
② （どうぞ、）よろしくお願いします。／Please treat me well.
③ （どうぞ、）よろしくお願いいたします。／Please treat me well. (most polite)
④ こちらこそ。／Likewise — the pleasure is mine.
(3) Introducing a third party
When introducing a third party to someone, you can first say “紹介します”, then give the specific introduction.
“紹介します” is a verb sentence meaning “let me introduce”. Japanese often omits the subject; the same is true in verb
sentences — here the subject “私は” is omitted, and the sentence consists only of the verb “紹介します”.
Next, when giving the specific introduction, you can gesture toward the person being introduced while saying “〇〇
さんです”; the subject can be omitted here. If you don't omit the subject, you can use the pattern “こちらは〇〇
さんです”. “こちら” means “this person”, with a polite, formal tone.
① 紹介します。（こちらは）ジョージさんです。／Let me introduce you. (This
is) George.
（4）そうですか。
This is a common reply for taking up what the other person said in conversation, equivalent to “is that so?”. “そうです
か” can be said with falling or rising intonation at the end. Generally, the final intonation falls,
taking up the other person's statement and meaning “I see” (as in example ①). When the final intonation rises, it expresses
doubt about what the other person said (as in example ②). For example:
① A: ジョージさんはアメリカ人で、経済学部の三年生です。／George is American, a third-year student in the economics department.
can, and a third-year student in the economics department.
B：そうですか。（↘）／I see.
② A: ジョージさんは日本人です。／George is Japanese.
B：そうですか。（↗）／Oh really?
source_file: 初级上/1.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第5课.md

title: ko-so-a-do demonstratives
body_lines: The ko-so-a-do words are four groups of demonstratives beginning with こ, そ, あ, and ど respectively,
used to point to things, places, or directions (see Table 6-1), translatable as "this ...", "that ..."
"that ... (over there)", and "which ...". Although both "so-series" and "a-series" words can be rendered "that ...",
they must be distinguished in actual use.
When the speaker and listener are far apart, the speaker uses "so-series" words for things or directions closer to the
listener. "A-series" words generally refer to third-party things or directions far from both the speaker and the
listener.
Table 6-1: ko-so-a-do demonstratives
Things  Places  Directions
Proximal これ ここ こちら
Medial それ そこ そちら
Distal あれ あそこ あちら
Interrogative どれ どこ どちら
① A：それは何ですか。／What is that?
B：（これは）日本のお菓子です。／(This is) a Japanese sweet.
② A：中村さんのかばんはどこですか。／Where is Nakamura's bag?
B：あ、あそこです。部屋の中です。／Ah, over there. Inside the room.
③ A：ここは何のお店ですか。／What kind of shop is this?
B：ここはパン屋です。／It's a bakery.
Besides indicating direction, こちら / そちら / あちら / どちら can also refer to
places, people, or things, and are more polite and formal than これ / ここ / どれ / どこ.
④ A：あのう、すみません。お手洗いはどこですか。／Excuse me. Where is the
restroom?
B：こちらです。／This way.
When introducing someone, こちら is also used to be polite.
⑤ 紹介します。こちらは李さんです。／Let me introduce (you). This is Li.
source_file: 初级上/3.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第6课.md

title: Ｎも ＜also＞
body_lines: The particle も follows a noun and means "also". Note that when も marks the topic of a sentence,
it replaces は.
① 中村さんの部屋もここですか。／Is Nakamura's room here too?
② 張さんも中国人です。／Zhang is also Chinese.
③ 私もこの大学の学生です。／I am also a student at this university.
source_file: 初级上/3.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第6课.md

title: N と ＜and＞
body_lines: 「と」 is a particle of coordination, used to connect two or more nouns in a parallel relationship.
Usually translated as "and".
① 清華大学と北京大学は 中国の大学です。／Tsinghua University and Peking University are Chi-
nese universities.
② ここは李さんと中村さんの 教室です。／This is Li and Nakamura's classroom.
③ これは由加さんのユーザー名とパスワードです。／This is your (Yuka's) user-
name and password.
source_file: 初级上/3.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第6课.md

title: N (place) に N が あります／います。 <existence sentence I>
body_lines: This is the basic pattern of the "existence sentence". The particle に follows "N (place)" to mark the
"place of existence", like "in/at ..." in English. The particle が marks the subject that exists (N). The verbs あ
ります and います both mean "to exist", like "there is/are". Their negative
forms are ありません and いません. あります is mostly used for things that cannot move on their own;
います is used for animate beings such as people or animals that can move on their own.
① 1階にコンビニがあります。／There is a convenience store on the 1st floor.
② 教室に学生がいます。／There are students in the classroom.
③ 駅の近くに中村さんのアパートがあります。／Near the station is Nakamura's apartment.
source_file: 初级上/3.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第6课.md

title: N (place) には N が あります／います。 <existence sentence II>
body_lines: The particle は marks the topic. Generally, a Japanese sentence can take a part other than the predicate verb
and promote it to the topic of the sentence by adding the topic-marking particle. In the basic pattern "N (place) に N が
あります／います。", to make the place where something exists the topic of the sentence,
add the topic particle は after "N (place) に", giving the pattern:
N (place) には N が あります／います。 <existence sentence II>
① かばんには携帯があります。／There is a phone in the bag.
② コンビニの隣にはパン屋があります。／Next to the convenience store is a bakery.
source_file: 初级上/3.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第6课.md

title: N は N (place) に あります／います。 <existence sentence III>
body_lines: To make the thing that exists (i.e., the subject) the topic of the sentence, replace the subject particle が
with the topic particle は, giving the pattern:
N は N (place) に あります／います。 <existence sentence III>
① あのう、Wi-Fiはありますか。／Excuse me, is there Wi-Fi?
② 由加さんの部屋は、３階にあります。／Yuka's room is on the 3rd floor.
"N は N (place) に あります／います。 <existence III>" can also be interchanged with the previously learned
"N は N です" pattern, mostly in spoken style. Compared with "〜は〜にありま
す／います", "N は N です" simply omits the existence verb ありま
す or います, but the meaning is basically the same.
③ −1 A：あのう、病院はどこですか。／Where is the hospital?
B：銀行の前です。／In front of the bank.
③−2 A：あのう、病院はどこにありますか。／Where is the hospital?
B：銀行の前にあります。／It's in front of the bank.
④ −1 社長は今、会議室です。／The president is in the meeting room now.
④−2 社長は今、会議室にいます。／The president is in the meeting room now.
source_file: 初级上/3.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第6课.md

title: それから
body_lines: "それから" is a conjunction. As an independent word, a conjunction generally connects preceding and following sentences,
paragraphs, or words. "それから" generally has two meanings: one follows a preceding item and indicates
that the following item happens next, usually translated "then"; the "それから" in this lesson
expresses addition, equivalent to "also; in addition" in English.
① それから、これはわたしの携帯番号です。／Also, this is my phone number.
② それから、これ、ほんの気持ちです。／And also, this is just a small token.
③ 中村さん、李さん、それから、小林 さんは大学院生です。／Nakamura,
Li, and also Kobayashi are graduate students.
source_file: 初级上/3.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第6课.md

title: Common numbers (up to 100) and how to read telephone numbers
body_lines: (1) Readings of common Japanese numbers (up to 10) and how to read telephone numbers
Number  Reading
1 いち②
2 に①
3 さん⓪
4 よん① /し①
5 ご①
6 ろく②
7 なな① /しち②
8 はち②
9 きゅう① /く①
10 じゅう①
0 ゼロ① /れい①
Japanese telephone numbers are read digit by digit, for example:
090-8563-7074 ぜろきゅうぜろ はちごろくさん ななぜろななよん
To make telephone numbers easier to write down, Japanese phone numbers are customarily split with a "-" after the 3rd or 4th
digit. The "-" usually isn't read aloud, but some people do read it as の.
For example:
054-223-6669 ぜろごよんの ににさんの ろくろくろくきゅう
(2) Reading numbers up to 100
Two-digit readings are composed of the single-digit readings.

40 よんじゅう①
50 ごじゅう②
60 ろくじゅう③
70 ななじゅう②

90 きゅうじゅう①
