title: Ways to end a conversation
body_lines: Japanese people generally don't use "さようなら" when saying goodbye, because it has the nuance of
"farewell forever". Japanese people choose an appropriate way to end a conversation depending on the context. Here, using the patterns from this lesson
as examples, we explain a few common situations.
（１）お疲れ様でした。
This is a common Japanese greeting meaning "thank you for your hard work". お疲れ様でした is the past
form, used to show appreciation after someone has worked hard. Note that this greeting is generally not used
toward people of higher status. When it comes up in conversation, you can reply like this:
① A：お疲れ様でした。／Thanks for your hard work.
B：お疲れ様でした。（used between people of similar age or standing）／Thanks for your hard work.
② A：お疲れ様でした。／Thanks for your hard work.
B：ありがとうございました。（used toward someone of higher status）／Thank you.
（２）ゆっくり休んでください。
"ゆっくり" is an adverb meaning "slowly; at leisure". "休んでください" is made of the verb 休む
(to rest) plus the auxiliary てください meaning "please (do)". The ね at the end of the sentence
is a modal particle. The sentence means "please get some good rest".
Of course, if it is at night before bed, you can also use "お休みなさい"
(good night), learned in Lesson 1.
（３）ありがとうございました。
"ありがとうございました" is the past tense of "ありがとうございます", and is also
a common greeting for parting on formal occasions. Japanese people generally don't say "さ
ようなら" when parting, because "さようなら" is too formal and can imply "farewell forever". Instead,
you can end the conversation with "ありがとうございました", carrying the sense of "thank you very much for today".
source_file: 初级上/3.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第6课.md

title: Common expressions for giving small gifts
body_lines: In daily work and life, Japanese people have the custom of giving small gifts to those who look after them.
These gifts are usually small local specialties. Japanese people are very reserved when expressing feelings,
often saying "ほんの気持ちです" while handing over the gift. It means "(this is) just a little
token of my appreciation".
① 由加：これ、ほんの気持ちです。／This is just a small token (of my thanks).
中村：わざわざすみません。／Sorry to have made you go to the trouble.
source_file: 初级上/3.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第6课.md

title: Past tense of noun sentences (polite form)
body_lines: In this book, the first grammar we learned was the "noun predicate sentence" (see Lesson 5, Grammar Notes
1). We have already learned the affirmative and negative polite forms of noun predicate sentences. In this lesson,
we continue with the past-tense usage of noun predicate sentences (polite form). Summarized in Table 7-1.
Table 7-1: Conjugation of noun predicate sentences (polite form)
Tense | Affirmative | Negative
Nです。 Nではありません。
Present / future
例：学生です。 例：学生ではありません。
Nでした。 Nではありませんでした。
Past
例：学生でした。 例：学生ではありませんでした。
(In spoken language, “では” can be replaced by “じゃ”)
① 昨日、日本語の試験でした。／Yesterday there was a Japanese exam.
② 三年前は 留学生でした。会社員ではありませんでした。／Three years ago (I) was an international
student. (At that time I) was not a company employee.
③ あの方は、ここの研修生でしたよ。／That person (once) was a trainee here.
④ 弟 はまだ小学生でした。／My brother was still an elementary school student (then).
source_file: 初级上/5.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第7课.md

title: Tenses of verb sentences (polite form)
body_lines: In contrast to the noun predicate sentences discussed earlier (noun sentences end with です to form a polite sentence),
verb-final sentences end with ます to form a polite sentence. ます is the affirmative polite form of a verb in the present or fu-
ture tense. Taking the verb 来ます as an example, the usage of polite verb sentences in various tenses
is summarized in Table 7-2.
Table 7-2: Conjugation of verb sentences (polite form)
Tense | Affirmative | Negative
Vます。 Vません。
Present · future
例：来ます。 例：来ません。
Vました。 Vませんでした。
Past
例：来ました。 例：来ませんでした。
① 兄は、今、アメリカにいます。／My older brother is in America now.
② 昨日、ジョージさんのお姉さんが来ました。／Yesterday, George's older sister came.
③ ２年前、ここに大学はありませんでした。／Two years ago, there was no university here.
source_file: 初级上/5.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第7课.md

title: Interrogative + が <marking the subject>
body_lines: The case particle が follows a noun to mark the "subject". When an interrogative word is the subject,
it must be marked with が, and the answer must also use が. When an interrogative is the subject, the particle
は cannot be used.
① A：研究室に誰がいますか。／Who is in the lab?
B：マイケルさんと先生がいます。／Michael and the teacher are there.
② どれが李さんのスマホですか。／Which one is your (Li's) phone?
③ A：どなたが（×は）日本語の先生ですか。／Who is the Japanese teacher?
B：あの方が（×は）日本語の先生です。／That person is the Japanese teacher.
source_file: 初级上/5.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第7课.md

title: Japanese "pre-noun adjectivals" (rentaishi)
body_lines: "この" "その" "あの" "どの" are "pre-noun adjectivals" and cannot be used independently. They can only precede a
noun, indicating and qualifying the person or thing referred to; they belong to the ko-so-a-do word family.
① 弟 さんはどの大学にいますか。／Which university is your brother at?
② 私の部屋はあの建物の2階です。／My room is on the 2nd floor of that building.
"Pre-noun adjectival" is one of the Japanese parts of speech. As the name suggests, it is "a word that connects to a substantive".
That is, a substantive (i.e., a noun) must follow it. For example:
The Japanese for "This is my computer" should be:
③-1. （○）これは私のパソコンです。／This is my computer.
③-2. （×）このは私のパソコンです。
In ③-2, "この" is a pre-noun adjectival, so a substantive must follow it, not the particle は. As for "this
computer is mine", the Japanese is:
④-1. （○）このパソコンは私のです。／This computer is mine.
④-2. （×）これパソコンは私のです。
"This computer" must be formed with the pre-noun adjectival この followed by パソコン, while in ④-2 "こ
れ" and "パソコン" are both substantives and cannot be connected.
source_file: 初级上/5.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第7课.md

title: だけ ＜limitation＞
body_lines: The particle だけ follows a noun or quantifier to express limitation; can be translated as "only", "just".
① A：経営学部の留学生は何人ですか。／How many international students are there in the business school?
B：5人です。アジア人は、私だけです。／There are five. The only Asian is my-
self.
② 地震は一回だけではありません。／It won't be just one earthquake.
③ 朝ごはんはりんごだけでした。／Breakfast was only an apple.
source_file: 初级上/5.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第7课.md

title: N の N <appositive>
body_lines: In previous lessons we learned to use の to connect two nouns, expressing possession (e.g., 私の本)
or attribute (e.g., 日本語の本). In this lesson, の expresses an appositive relation between nouns,
meaning the nouns before and after の refer to the same thing. In apposition, the noun before の usually denotes a relation-
ship or property, while the noun after の is usually a proper noun, such as a person's name.
① そして、 弟 のハチです。／And this is my little brother, Hachi.
② こちらは課長の長谷川さんです。／This is section chief Hasegawa.
③ 紹介します。クラスメートのジョージさんです。／Let me introduce (him). (This)
is my classmate George.
source_file: 初级上/5.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第7课.md

title: Sentence + よ <assertion; calling attention>
body_lines: The particle よ is used at the end of a sentence to express the speaker's assertion, declaration, and other emphatic nuances. The sentence-final
よ is mostly read with rising intonation.
① A：これはいつの写真ですか。／When was this photo taken?
B：10年前の写真ですよ。／It's a photo from 10 years ago.
② A：中村さんもこの大学の学生ですか。／Is Nakamura also a student at this university?
B：そうですよ。／Yes, that's right.
source_file: 初级上/5.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第7课.md

title: Japanese family terms and introducing family members
body_lines: In Japanese, when it comes to one's family situation, inside and outside must be clearly distinguished. For the other party's situation
use respectful terms; for your own, use humble terms. This distinction between respectful and humble terms effectively
avoids modifiers like "your" and "my", which fits the Japanese habit of rarely using 私 or あなた,
and also makes the language more concise and polite.
（１）ご家族
Before some nouns made of two kanji — "Sino-Japanese words" — the prefix ご can be added
as an honorific or to show respect, mostly referring to the listener's situation, e.g. ご意見 (your opinion), ご
住所 (your address). "Your family" can be said directly as ご家族. As in this lesson's dialogue, it can also be expressed as 李さんのご家族 or 中村さんのご家族.
(2) Kinship terms
Kinship terms in Japanese also require special attention. For other people's family members use respectful terms, and
for your own relatives use humble forms. Table 7-3 summarizes Japanese kinship terms in three
cases: "humble" is used when introducing your own relatives to people outside the family, as in example ①;
"in-family address" is what family members use to address each other, as in example ②; "respectful"
is what people outside the family use to address someone's relatives, as in example ③.
Table 7-3: Kinship terms
Humble  In-family  Respectful
爸爸 父①② お父さん② お父さん②
Mother 母① お母さん② お母さん②
哥哥 兄① お兄さん② お兄さん②
姐姐 姉⓪ お姉さん② お姉さん②
Wife 妻①／家内① 奥さん①
丈夫 夫 ⓪／主人① ご主人②
弟弟 弟 ④ 弟 さん⓪
妹妹 妹 ④ 妹 さん⓪
Grandfather 祖父① おじいさん② おじいさん②
奶奶 祖母① おばあさん② おばあさん②
阿姨 叔母⓪ おばさん⓪ おばさん⓪
叔叔 叔父⓪ おじさん⓪ おじさん⓪
Son 息子⓪ 息子さん⓪
Daughter 娘③ 娘さん⓪／お嬢さん②
① 10年前の写真ですよ。弟 はまだ小学生でした。／This is a photo from 10 years ago.
My brother was still an elementary school student.
② 娘：これ、お母さんの？／Is this yours, Mom?
母：うん。／Yeah.
③ 弟 さんは今おいくつですか。／How old is your brother now?
(3) How to talk about family size
You can ask or describe family size in the following two ways:
① A：（〜さんは）何人家族ですか。／How many people are in your family?
B：（私は）3人家族です。／I have a family of three.
② A：〜さんのご家族は何人ですか。／How many people are in your family?
B：私の家族は3人です。／My family has three people.
Japanese also has the concept of quantifiers; the number of family members can be expressed with a numeral plus the counter 人. But here, special
attention must be paid to the readings of 人, as follows:
1人 ひとり② 7人 しちにん②／ななにん②
2人 ふたり③ 8人 はちにん②
3人 さんにん③ 9人 きゅうにん①／くにん②
4人 よにん② 10人 じゅうにん①
5人 ごにん②
6人 ろくにん②
Interrogative: 何人①
source_file: 初级上/5.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第7课.md

title: How to talk about age in Japanese
body_lines: When asking someone's age, you can use the following:
① おいくつですか。／How old are you?
It is worth noting that the interrogative いくつ means "how old". As mentioned earlier, before "Sino-Japanese words"
the prefix ご can be added as an honorific or to show respect, mostly referring to the listener's situation, such as
ご家族. Before native Japanese words like いくつ, the prefix お is usually added to show
respect or politeness.
Similar to the number-of-people expression, Japanese forms age expressions with a numeral plus the age counter,
as follows:
１歳 いっさい① ６歳 ろくさい②
２歳 にさい① ７歳 ななさい②
３歳 さんさい① ８歳 はっさい①
４歳 よんさい① ９歳 きゅうさい①
５歳 ごさい① 10歳 じ（ゅ）っさい①
18歳 じゅうはっさい③
20歳 はたち① にじ（ゅ）っさい②
24歳 にじゅう・よんさい①＋①
source_file: 初级上/5.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第7课.md

title: Other common spoken expressions in this lesson
body_lines: （１）いえ
Expresses negation; more colloquial than いいえ.
（２）そして
"そして" can connect sentences or words, expressing progression or addition. Can be translated as "and,
also, then" etc.
（３）ハチ君、かわいい！
"-くん" is mostly attached to the names of close male friends younger than oneself. It is more casual than "-さ
ん". In the workplace, male bosses can also be seen using "-くん" to address young female subordi-
nates. In this text, "ハチ" is a small dog that Nakamura regards as family, so
Yuka uses the address "ハチ君", showing affection.
Also, かわいい is an adjective, used to describe people or things as "cute; pretty".
The usage of adjectives will be studied in detail in Lesson 9.
source_file: 初级上/5.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第7课.md

title: N を <marking the object>
body_lines: The particle を follows a noun to mark the object. Japanese is an SOV (subject-object-verb)
language, where the predicate verb usually comes at the end of the sentence and the object comes earlier, marked with
"ください" is the imperative form of the verb くださる (to give), equivalent to "please give me
...". "Nをください。" is mostly used when shopping or ordering food.
① 水族館の入 場券をください。／I'd like an admission ticket to the aquarium, please.
② チーズバーガーセットをください。／I'd like a cheeseburger set, please.
③ ビールをください。／A beer, please.
To express "I also want ...", use the particle も meaning "also". も and を
cannot be used together; も must replace を.
④ それから、ホットコーヒーもください。／And also, a hot coffee please.
source_file: 初级上/7.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第8课.md

title: N を (quantity) ください。
body_lines: To express the quantity you want to buy, place the quantifier before the verb ください. For
quantifier expressions, see this lesson's "Expanding Expressions" 1-(2).
① A：この水族館の入 場 券を3枚ください。／Three admission tickets to the aquarium, please.
B：はい、3000円です。／Certainly, that will be 3,000 yen.
② チーズバーガーセットを一つください。／One cheeseburger set, please.
③ A：いらっしゃいませ。／Welcome.
B：あのう、これを2本ください。／Um, two of these, please.
④ シャツを３枚ください。／Three shirts, please.
In Japanese, quantifiers generally come before the verb. For example:
⑤ 兄が2人います。／I have two older brothers.
⑥ スマホが２台あります。／There are two phones.
source_file: 初级上/7.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第8课.md

title: N でお願いします。
body_lines: The verb お願いします in this pattern means "I beg; please" and is a courteous, polite
expression; when asking someone to do something for you, お願いします can directly re-
place a specific verb. In examples ① and ②, お願いします replaces the verb ください.
① ホットコーヒーをお願いします。／A hot coffee, please.
② これを4つお願いします。／Four of these, please.
The particle で follows a noun to indicate the means or method of the following action. Combined with お願いします,
it forms the means by which you ask someone to do something.
③ Sサイズでお願いします。／A small (size), please.
④ Sサイズのコーヒーをお願いします。／A small coffee, please.
In this lesson's "Model Conversation" pattern (example ③), the object-marking case particle を
is replaced by で. The particle で after a noun marks the "state". Example ④ rather emphasizes
pointing out "I want a small coffee". Example ③ appears in a conversational context, where a hot coffee
has already been mentioned. So when asked "what size?", answering "Sサイズで" emphasizes that the way of buy-
ing the coffee is the small size. This expression is more idiomatic and natural. Also:
⑤ （when paying）アリペイでお願いします。／Please (process the payment) with Alipay.
⑥ （when asking the other party to contact you）Eメールでお願いします。／Please contact me by email.
source_file: 初级上/7.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第8课.md

title: N でございます。
body_lines: The assertive auxiliary でございます is the formal version of です. Formal style is mostly
used on formal occasions such as speeches or international conferences, or by service-industry staff toward customers. When used,
the subject is generally oneself or one's own side's people or things; it generally cannot be used for the respected listener
or their people or things.
① エレベーターはこちらでございます。／The elevator is this way.
② 私が担当者でございます。／I am the person in charge.
③ （when Tanaka's colleague introduces their own manager to the client company）部 長 の田中でご
ざいます。／This is Manager Tanaka.
④ A（person from an outside company）：田中部長は、今日、お休みですか。／Is Manager Tanaka off
today?
B（Tanaka's colleague）：はい、休みでございます。／Yes, he is off today.
source_file: 初级上/7.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第8课.md

title: どうなさいますか。
body_lines: The interrogative どう is equivalent to "how". なさいます is the honorific verb for する
(to do); using なさいます makes the speaker's tone more polite and formal.
"どうなさいますか" is equivalent to "How would you like it?" "What would you like to do?"
mostly used by service-industry staff. For example:
① A：ホットコーヒーのサイズはどうなさいますか。／What size would you like for your hot coffee?
B：Lサイズでお願いします。／A large, please.
When the interrogative どう serves as the predicate, it can be followed by ですか to form the wh-question "〜はどうで
すか。", used to ask the listener's opinion about the thing the subject refers to. For example:
② このコーヒーはどうですか。／How is this coffee?
③ 清華大学はどうですか。／How is Tsinghua University?
④ 最近はどうですか。／How have you been lately?
source_file: 初级上/7.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第8课.md

title: Numbers over 100 and quantifiers
body_lines: (1) How to say numbers over 100
Table 8-1: Numbers over 100
Units  Readings to note
百 100 ひゃく②
300 さんびゃく①
600 ろっぴゃく④
800 はっぴゃく④
千 1000 せん①
3000 さんぜん③
8000 はっせん③
万 10000 いちまん③
Examples
110 ひゃくじゅう②+①
305 さんびゃくご①+①
1108 せんひゃくはち①+②+②
1800 せんはっぴゃく①+④
(2) Quantifiers
Like Chinese, Japanese has "quantifiers", usually composed of a numeral plus a counter. Japanese
"counters" are not as varied as Chinese ones and are mostly classified by shape and size. Table 8-2 lists the more commonly used
quantifiers. Note that because of the different readings of the preceding numerals, some Japanese quantifiers undergo
sound changes.
Table 8-2: Common Japanese quantifiers and their readings
Quantifier  Meaning  Readings/usage to note  Interrogative
〜 え 円 ん 日元 ひ 百 ゃくえ 円 ん ⓪、 せ 千 んえ 円 ん ①、 い 一 ちま 万 んえ 円 ん ⓪ いくら①
ほん いっぽん さんぼん ろっぽん はっぽん じ（ゅ）っ ぽん なんぼん
〜本 long thin objects: 1本①, 3本①, 6本①, 8本①, 10本①; 何本①
Mostly used for long, slender items
〜つ items: 一つ② 二つ③ 三つ③ 四つ③ 五つ② いくつ①
／〜個 六つ③ 七つ② 八つ③ 九つ② 十① 何個①
"〜つ" only has forms up to ten. "〜個" is unlimited.
〜枚 sheets/items; mostly for flat, thin objects; 何枚①
〜匹 small animals: 1匹④ 3匹① 4匹① 6匹④ 8匹⓪ 何匹①
〜台 machines/vehicles; mostly for cars and machines; 何台①
〜歳 years of age. See Lesson 7 "Expanding Expressions" 2; 何歳①
Ages up to ten can also use "〜つ"; いくつ①
source_file: 初级上/7.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第8课.md

title: Common expressions for shopping, ordering, and paying
body_lines: (1) Step 1: State your needs
When ordering at a restaurant or shopping at a store, you can use "Nをください。" to say "I'd like ..."
"please give me ..." to state your needs. You can also use the pattern "Nをお願いします。", which
is more polite and courteous.
① ビールをください。／A beer, please.
② ヨーグルトをお願いします。／Yogurt, please.
(2) Step 2: State the means or method of fulfilling your needs
After stating your needs, if you want to add the means by which you want them fulfilled, you can use "Nで
お願いします。".
① コーヒーはSサイズでお願いします。／For the coffee, a small size please.
② （when asking the clerk to wrap a gift）リボンはゴールドでお願いします。／For the rib-
bon, gold please.
(3) Step 3: Payment
You can use an action noun followed by "お願いします。" to politely ask
someone to do something for you. For example:
① 客： お会計、お願いします。／The check, please.
店員：かしこまりました。／Certainly.
You can also use "Nでお願いします。" to state the payment method. For example:
② 現金でお願いします。／(I'll pay) in cash.
③ カードでお願いします。／I'll pay by card.
④ アリペイでお願いします。／(I'll pay) with Alipay.
When paying in cash, the receiver usually says "〜円のお返しです" when giving change.
⑤ 1 １０円のお返しです。／Here is your 10 yen change.
source_file: 初级上/7.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第8课.md

title: Common replies in this lesson to requests or instructions from others
body_lines: （１）わかりました。
To respond positively to a request or instruction, you can use "わかりました。" or "はい、わ
かりました。" — meaning "Understood", "Got it".
① A：ゆっくり休んでくださいね。／Please get some good rest.
B：わかりました。／Got it.
② A：明日もお願いします。／I'm counting on you tomorrow too.
B：はい、わかりました。／Yes, understood.
（２）かしこまりました。
This is a set phrase, translatable as "Understood", "Certainly". It is mostly used by subordinates giving a positive reply
to a superior's instruction. It is more formal and polite than "わかりました。", and is mostly used by service-industry staff.
① 客：カードでお願いします。／I'll pay by card.
店員：かしこまりました。／Certainly.
"はい" has many uses in Japanese; it can express affirmation, as in example ①. In this lesson's conversation, "は
い" is said while handing money to the other party, with the nuance of drawing their attention, as in examples ② and ③.
① A：新入生ですか。／Are you a new student?
B：はい、そうです。／Yes, that's right.
② A： ７ ９ ０円です。／That's 790 yen.
B：はい。／Here you go.
③ はい、私の名刺です。／Here, this is my business card.
（4）大丈夫です。
"大丈夫です。" originally means "no problem; it's all right". In recent years, modern Japanese has derived
another new usage: declining someone's invitation or kind offer, mostly used by young
people.
① （when the clerk asks whether you have a points card and offers to add points）大丈夫です。／No thanks, I'm fine.
② （when a friend offers you snacks but you don't really want any）ありがとう、大 丈 夫で
す。／ Thanks, I'm fine.
source_file: 初级上/7.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第8课.md

title: Adjective predicate sentences
body_lines: Adjectives as predicates express states or constant properties. In Japanese, adjectives are divided into two types: type I
adjectives (ending in い) and type II adjectives (in Japanese "school grammar" type II adjectives are called "adjec-
tive verbs"). The polite non-past forms of adjective predicate sentences differ according to the type:
(1) Polite non-past (present or future) affirmative forms of adjective predicate sentences
Type I adjective: A ＋ です。
Ⅰ
Type II adjective: A ＋ です。
Ⅱ
(2) Polite non-past (present or future) negative forms of adjective predicate sentences
Type I adjective: A い→く＋ありません。
Ⅰ
Type II adjective: A ＋では（じゃ）ありません。
Ⅱ
Table 9-1: Non-past conjugations of adjective predicate sentences (polite form)
Adjective type | Tense | Affirmative (polite) | Negative (polite)
Type I adjective | Present/Future | 高いです。 | 高くありません。
（例：高い）
Type II adjective | Present/Future | 静かです。 | 静かでは（じゃ）ありません。
(example: 静か)
(In spoken language, “では” can be replaced by “じゃ”)
① 東京は寒いです。／Tokyo is cold.
② あの映画は面白くありません。／That movie is not interesting.
③ 先生は親切です。／The teacher is kind.
④ 日本語は簡単ではありません。／Japanese is not simple.
Note that the adjective いい must first be changed to よ
い before conjugating. For example, the non-past negative form of いいです is よ
くありません”。
⑤ 成績はよくありません。／(My) grades are not good.
source_file: 初级上/9.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第9课.md

title: N は N が〜。
body_lines: This is a typical expression favored by Japanese speakers, unlike what Chinese speakers are used to. The particle
は marks the topic of the sentence (also called the "big subject"), and が marks the subject (the "small subject"). In the pattern "A は
B が X です", the statement is mainly about the topic A (A is usually the whole of a person or thing),
B is usually a part of A, and "B が X です" expresses A's characteristic. For example:
A B X
① 象 - 鼻 - 長い → 象は鼻が長いです。／Elephants have long noses.
② 富士山 -形 - いい → 富士山は形がいいです。／Mt. Fuji has a nice shape.
③ 今日 -天気 - いい → 今日は天気がいいです。／The weather is nice today.
④ 彼女 -性格 - 明るい→ 彼女は性格が明るいです。／She has a cheerful personality.
source_file: 初级上/9.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第9课.md

title: あまり／そんなに形容詞（否定）
body_lines: The degree adverbs あまり and そんなに can both be paired with the negative form of adjectives,
equivalent to "not very ...", "not that ..." in English.
① A：東京は寒いですか。／Is Tokyo cold?
B：いいえ、あまり寒くありません。／No, it's not very cold.
② 日本語はそんなに難しくありません。／Japanese is not that difficult.
③ このパソコンはそんなに遅くありません。／This computer is not that slow.
source_file: 初级上/9.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第9课.md

title: Sentence + から。 <cause-effect>
body_lines: The particle から is used at the end of a sentence to express a reason, equivalent to "because ..." (sentence)
① （中村さんは）とても真面目ですから。／Because (Nakamura) is very serious.
② アイスクリームがいいです。暑いですから。／Ice cream would be nice. Because it's hot
(outside).
③ A：寒いですね。／It's cold, isn't it?
B：そうですね。今日は雪ですから。／That's right. Because it's snowing today.
source_file: 初级上/9.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第9课.md

title: N は どうですか。 <asking about the nature of things>
category: asking about the nature of things
body_lines: The interrogative どう means "how". "N は どうですか" is used to ask about
the nature of something or the listener's view of what the subject refers to; it can be answered with an adjective predicate sentence.
① A：日本の留学生活はどうですか。／How is life as an international student in Japan?
B：順 調ですよ。／It's going well.
② A：日本語はどうですか。／How is Japanese?
B：難しいです。／It's hard.
③ A：この映画はどうですか。／How is this movie?
B：とても面白いです。／It's really interesting.
source_file: 初级上/9.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第9课.md

title: Sentence + よ。 <assertion; calling attention>
body_lines: The particle よ is used at the end of a sentence to express the speaker's assertion or declaration, an emphatic nuance.
① 中村さんのおかげですよ。／It's all thanks to Nakamura.
② 山羊座の人はみんな真面目ですよ。／Capricorns are all serious, you know.
③ 日本語はそんなに難しくありませんよ。／Japanese isn't that hard, you know.
source_file: 初级上/9.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第9课.md

title: Sentence + ね。 <mild exclamation (particle ね II)>
body_lines: When the particle ね at the end of a sentence expresses mild exclamation, it is read with falling intonation; depending on the nuance, it can also be lengthened
to ねえ.
① 由加ちゃんはすごいですね。（↘）／Yuka, you're amazing.
② この洋服、かわいいですね。（↘）／These clothes are cute, aren't they.
③ 由加ちゃんのこのスマホケース、かわいいですね。（↘）／Yuka, this phone case of yours
is so cute.
source_file: 初级上/9.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第9课.md

title: The modal particles よ and ね
body_lines: Compared with Chinese, one major feature of Japanese is the frequent use of modal particles. But many begin-
ners are not used to using modal particles, or often misuse them. Table 9-2 summarizes the usages of the modal particles
よ and ね learned so far.
Table 9-2: Uses of the modal particles よ and ね
Particle  Meaning  Example  Usage  Intonation
A：日本の 留 学生活はどう  Information known to the speaker but unknown to the listener.
Assertion;
よ ですか。  Or information the speaker uses to empha- ↗
call attention
B： 順 調 ですよ。  size information already known to the listener.
Information the speaker is unsure of but the listener al-
Confirmation  こんにちは。中村さんですね。 ↗
ready knows.
Exclaiming over an existing fact (usually also known
to the listener). Depending
Exclamation  由加ちゃんはすごいですね。 ↘
on the nuance, ね can also
be lengthened to ねえ.
source_file: 初级上/9.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第9课.md

title: How to say dates
body_lines: (1) Years
The numeric part of a year follows the regular number readings. Add 年 after it.
2000年 にせんねん⓪
1999年 せん①きゅうひゃく①きゅうじゅう①きゅうねん①
2025年 にせん②にじゅう①ごねん⓪
Interrogative: 何年 なんねん①
(2) Months
1月 いちがつ④ 2月 にがつ③
3月 さんがつ① 4月 しがつ③
5月 ごがつ① 6月 ろくがつ④
7月 しちがつ④ 8月 はちがつ④
9月 くがつ① 10月 じゅうがつ④
11月 じゅういちがつ⑥ 12月 じゅうにがつ⑤
Interrogative: 何月 なんがつ①
(3) Days of the month
1日 ついたち④ 2日 ふつか⓪
3日 みっか⓪ 4日 よっか⓪
5日 いつか⓪ 6日 むいか⓪
7日 なのか⓪ 8日 ようか⓪
9日 ここのか④ 10日 とおか⓪
The readings for the 1st–10th are special; from the 11th on, 日 is read にち.
11日 じゅういちにち⑥ 12日 じゅうににち⑤
13 日 じゅうさんにち③ 14日 じゅうよっか①＋⓪
15 日 じゅうごにち①＋① 16日 じゅうろくにち⑥
17 日 じゅうしちにち⑥ 18日 じゅうはちにち⑥
19 日 じゅうくにち①＋① 20日 はつか⓪
24 日 にじゅうよっか①＋⓪ 29日 にじゅうくにち①＋①
Interrogative: 何日 なんにち①
(4) Days of the week
星期一 月曜日 げつようび③
星期二 火曜日 かようび②
Wednesday 水曜日 すいようび③
星期四 木曜日 もくようび③
星期五 金曜日 きんようび③
星期六 土曜日 どようび②
星期日 日曜日 にちようび③
Interrogative: 何曜日 なんようび③
source_file: 初级上/9.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第9课.md

title: Common spoken expressions in this lesson
body_lines: （１）中村さんのおかげですよ。
This is a very polite expression meaning "it's all thanks to Nakamura". You can use "〜
さんのおかげです" to express gratitude to someone.
① 先生：合格、おめでとう。／Congratulations on passing the exam!
学生：ありがとうございます。先生のおかげです。／Thank you. It's all thanks to you,
teacher.
（２）どういたしまして。
This is the reply to "ありがとうございます", meaning "you're welcome". "どういたしま
して" sounds rather formal. In a relaxed atmosphere, you can reply to thanks with "いいえ",
which sounds more natural.
① 由加：中村さんのおかげですよ。いろいろありがとう。／It's all thanks to you, Nakamura. Thank you for everything.
中村：どういたしまして。／You're welcome.
② A：ありがとう。／Thanks.
B：いいえ。／Not at all.
（３）どうしてですか。
The interrogative どうして means "why". It can be followed by ですか to directly ask for a reason.
In this lesson, Yuka guesses whether Nakamura might be a Capricorn, and Nakamura wonders why Yuka asks that,
so she asks "どうしてですか。" in Japanese, meaning "why do you ask?".
（４）いえいえ。
"いえいえ" is also a colloquial form of "いいえ", with a stronger tone than "いえ", mostly used
to humbly respond to someone's compliment.
① A：Bさんは本当に性格がいいですね。／You really have a nice personality.
B：いえいえ、そんなことはありませんよ。／No, no, that's not true.
（５）誕生日パーティーをしましょう。
It means "let's have a birthday party". "〜しましょう" means "let's (do) ... together";
this grammar will be learned in Lesson 14.
① A：この後、お茶をしましょう。／Let's have tea later.
B：いいですね。／Sounds good.
source_file: 初级上/9.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第9课.md

title: Adjective-predicate sentences (polite) — past tense
body_lines: Lesson 9 covered the non-past tense of adjectives (polite); here we learn the past tense of adjective-predicate sentences (polite).
The past-tense usage of adjective-predicate sentences (polite) requires different conjugations depending on the type of adjective,
as follows:
(1) Affirmative past form of adjective-predicate sentences (polite)
Type I adjectives: A い → かった + です。
Ⅰ
Type II adjectives: A + でした。
Ⅱ
(2) Negative past form of adjective-predicate sentences (polite)
Type I adjectives: A い → く + ありませんでした。
Ⅰ
Type II adjectives: A + ではありませんでした。
Ⅱ
Table 10-1: Conjugation table of adjective-predicate sentences (polite)
Adjective type | Tense | Affirmative (polite) | Negative (polite)
Type I adjective | Present/Future | 高いです。 | 高くありません。
(e.g. 高い) | Past | 高かったです。 | 高くありませんでした。
Type II adjective | Present/Future | 静かです。 | 静かでは（じゃ）ありません。
(e.g. 静か) | Past | 静かでした。 | 静かでは（じゃ）ありませんでした。
(In spoken language, “では” can be replaced by “じゃ”)
① A: お客さんは多かったですか。／Were there many customers?
B: ううん、平日の昼間ですから、ばらばらでしたよ。／No, since it was a weekday
afternoon, (customers) were sparse.
② 子供の時、生活は豊かではありませんでした。／When I was a child, life was not affluent.
③ 10年前の家賃はそんなに高くありませんでした。／Rent ten years ago wasn't that
expensive.
source_file: 初级上/13.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第10课.md

title: The negative “ない”
body_lines: “ない” means “not; there is no”, and is a Type I adjective. It is also an “auxiliary adjective” attached
after adjectives to express negation. “ない” followed by “です” is fairly polite and can be interchanged with “ありません”.
You can memorize the following “formula”:
ありません。＝ないです。
Then the past tense of the two is:
ありませんでした。＝なかったです。
Based on this formula, the polite affirmative and negative forms of adjective-predicate sentences in each tense (called the “adjective
four quadrants” in this book) can be summarized in Table 10-2.
Table 10-2: Conjugation table of the adjective four quadrants (polite)
Adjective type | Tense | Affirmative (polite) | Negative (polite)
Type I adjective | Present/Future | 高いです。 | 高くありません。
（例：高い） 或：高くないです。
Past | 高かったです。 | 高くありませんでした。
或：高くなかったです。
Type II adjective | Present/Future | 静かです。 | 静かでは（じゃ）ありません。
(e.g. 静か) | Or: 静かでは（じゃ）ないです。
Past | 静かでした。 | 静かでは（じゃ）ありませんでした。
Or: 静かでは（じゃ）なかったです。
(In spoken language, “では” can be replaced by “じゃ”)
Similarly, noun-predicate sentences (polite) in each tense (called the “noun four quadrants” in this book) have the conjugation forms in Table 10-
Table 10-3: Conjugation table of the noun four quadrants (polite)
Part of speech | Tense | Affirmative | Negative
Noun | Present/Future | 学生です。 | 学生では（じゃ）ありません。
(e.g. 学生) | Or: 学生では（じゃ）ないです。
Past | 学生でした。 | 学生では（じゃ）ありませんでした。
Or: 学生では（じゃ）なかったです。
(In spoken language, “では” can be replaced by “じゃ”)
source_file: 初级上/13.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第10课.md

title: The continuative form of adjectives <adjective ren'yokei>
body_lines: The “continuative” in Japanese, also called “ren'yokei”, is “the form for connecting predicates”. The “continuative” is used at pause points
within a sentence, where the parts before and after the pause are mostly in a parallel, sequential relation. Sometimes we use two, three, or even more
adjectives to describe the qualities of the same thing. When these adjectives are in a parallel relation, the continuative
form of the adjective (i.e. its second ren'yokei) is needed. Different types of adjectives have different continuative forms, as follows:
Type I adjectives: A い → く + て, ...
Ⅰ
Type II adjectives: A + で, ...
Ⅱ
① 映画の主人公は背が高くて、魅力的です。／The movie's protagonist is tall and attractive.
② 昨日の試験問題は複雑で、難しかったです。／Yesterday's exam questions were complicated and difficult.
Note: the continuative form is chosen according to the part of speech of the first item only, not determined by the second. For example:
③−1 映画の主人公は背が高くて、かっこいいです。／The movie's protagonist is tall and cool.
③−2 映画の主人公は背が高くて、魅力的です。／The movie's protagonist is tall and
very attractive.
“背が高い” is a Type I adjective; whether it is followed by a Type I adjective (like “かっこいい” in ③-1)
or a Type II adjective (like “魅力的” in ③-2) does not affect the continuative form of “高い”. That is, the continuative form of the first item “背が
高い” is determined solely by its own part of speech and is unaffected by what follows.
In addition, tense is determined by the sentence-final predicate; the continuative part does not need to mark tense. For example:
④ 昨日の映画の主人公は背が高くて、魅力的でした。／The protagonist of yesterday's movie was
tall and attractive.
source_file: 初级上/13.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第10课.md

title: N まで <end point>
body_lines: The particle “まで” follows a noun and indicates an end point, equivalent to “until; up to; as far as”. “まで”

can follow a noun with temporal meaning or a time noun, as in this lesson, or a place noun to indicate the end point of a location. “まで” can also be followed directly by the copula “です” to end the sentence, forming a noun-predi-
cate sentence.
① わたしは昨日、遅くまで日本語の試験でした。／Yesterday my Japanese exam went until late.
② 今日の授業はここまでです。／That's all for today's class.
③ あの歌手のライブツアーは来月20日までです。／That singer's concert tour runs until the
20th of next month.
source_file: 初级上/13.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第10课.md

title: 全然 + adjective (negative)
body_lines: Like “あまり” learned in the previous lesson, “全然” is also a degree adverb and must be paired
with the negative form of an adjective; it can be translated as “(not) at all ...”.
① A: 昨日の試験は難 しかったですか。／Was yesterday's exam difficult?
B: 全然難しくなかったですよ。／It wasn't difficult at all.
② わたしは運動が全然好きではありません。／I don't like exercise at all.
③ 彼女の料理は全然美味しくありません。／Her cooking isn't good at all.
In spoken language, “全然” alone can also express “not at all”, “none at all”.
④ A: 日本語の試験は難 しかったですか。／Was the Japanese exam difficult?
B: ううん、全然。／Not at all.
source_file: 初级上/13.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第10课.md

title: N とか ＜examples＞
body_lines: The particle “とか” follows a noun and is used to give examples. “とか” is mostly used in spoken conversation; it can be used once in a sentence
or appear multiple times in the same sentence. When “とか” is used, the topic/subject particles “は”
and “が”, and the object particle “を”, can be omitted.
① A: どんな飲み物が好きですか。／What drinks do you like?
B: ミルクティーとか、コーラとか。／Milk tea, cola, things like that.
② 木曜日の午後以降とかはどうですか。／How about, say, Thursday afternoon or later?
source_file: 初级上/13.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第10课.md

title: Telling time
body_lines: Japanese time is mainly expressed with “-時”, “-分”, and “-半”, corresponding to “o'clock”, “minutes”, and “half past”. The specific read-
ings are as follows:
１時 いちじ② ８時 はちじ②
２時 にじ① ９時 くじ①
３時 さんじ① 10時 じゅうじ①
４時 よじ① 11時 じゅういちじ④
５時 ごじ① 12時 じゅうにじ③
６時 ろくじ② 0時 れいじ①
７時 しちじ② 何時 なんじ①
5分 ごふん①
10分 じ（ゅ）っぷん①
15分 じゅうごふん①③
20分 にじ（ゅ）っぷん②
25分 にじゅう・ごふん①+①
30分 さんじ（ゅ）っぷん③
−半 はん①
何分 なんぷん①
source_file: 初级上/13.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第10课.md

title: About making suggestions
body_lines: (1) Suggestion method 1: N はどうですか。<suggestion II>
Without using a verb, you can make a suggestion with the pattern “N はどうですか”. Here
N is the content of the suggestion, such as the time of an appointment, its content, or some recommended options. It means “How about ...?”.
① 来週はどうですか。／How about next week?
② 6時はどうですか。／How about 6 o'clock?
③ お茶はどうですか。／How about some tea?
④ 映画はどうですか。／How about a movie?
Review: Lesson 9 also covered another use of “N はどうですか” — do you remember it? (See
Lesson 9, Grammar 5 for details)
(2) Suggestion method 2: (いっしょに) N をしましょうか。
We have not yet formally studied the use of Japanese verbs; for now you can memorize the pattern “(いっ
しょに）〜をしましょうか” — “しましょうか” means “shall we (do together)?”.

The particle “を” marks the object of “do”. Attached to an action noun, it conveys inviting or suggesting doing something together, translated as “let's (do together) ...”. Here N is mostly a noun with
verbal meaning, such as “テニス”, “ダンス”, “勉強”.
① 映画の後、一緒にお茶をしましょうか。／After the movie, shall we go get some-
thing to drink together?
Here, “お茶をしましょうか” means “shall we have something to drink?”.
source_file: 初级上/13.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第10课.md

title: Ways to respond to suggestions
body_lines: (1) Agreeing
You can use the following sentences to express agreement with the other person's suggestion. Depending on the situation, you can add “ありがとう
ございます / thank you” to thank them for the suggestion or invitation.
① A：一緒にテニスをしましょうか。／Let's play tennis together.
B：いいですね。／Sounds good.
② はい、大丈夫です。／Yes, that's fine.
③ そうしましょう。／Let's do that.
（２）refusal; rejection
Japanese people also use the following sentences when declining a suggestion or invitation, such as “大丈夫で
す。”, “けっこうです。”, “ちょっと……”, “いいです。”, usually accompanied by an apologetic look
or a “すみません” of regret. Depending on the situation, you can also make another suggestion in return, for example:
① A：お茶はどうですか。／How about some tea?
B：あ、大丈夫です。ありがとうございます。／Ah, I'm fine. Thank you.
② A：明日、一緒に映画はどうですか。／How about seeing a movie together tomorrow?
B：すみません。ちょっと…今度はぜひ一緒に。／Sorry. It's a bit... Next time, let's definitely go together.
“今度” means “next time”. “ぜひ” is an adverb meaning “by all means; definitely”. After “今度はぜひ一緒
に”, the verb “映画を見る / watch a movie” is omitted. The particle “は” emphasizes the tone of “next time for
sure”. So even before you can use the specific verb, you can still use “今度
はぜひ一緒に” to mean “(not this time, but) next time let's definitely do it to-
gether”.
source_file: 初级上/13.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第10课.md

title: Common spoken responses in this lesson
body_lines: （1）よかったですね。
“よかった” is the past form of the adjective “いい”. Adding
the exclamatory particle “ね” after “よかったです” expresses happiness about what happened to the other person;
it can be translated as “That's great”, “Good for you”.
① A：先週の試験、どうでしたか。／How was last week's exam?
B：満点でしたよ。／I got full marks.
A：よかったですね！おめでとう。／That's great! Congratulations.
（2）まあ、なんとか。
The adverb “まあ” is mostly used in spoken language; it can stand alone or be used with a following predicate, expressing
basic agreement with what the other person said, translatable as “so-so”, “pretty good”, etc. This can be used
when someone asks you how things are going.
The adverb “なんとか” means “(though not as satisfying as hoped) somehow manageable”.
In spoken language, “なんとか” can be used alone or with a verb after it
(see Lesson 18 for details), with the meaning “to manage to ... somehow”, “finally ...”.
(3) “うん” and “ううん”
“うん” and “ううん” are the spoken forms of “はい” and “いいえ” respectively, used between people who are close,
to express agreement or denial. “うん” and “ううん” are generally not used toward superiors,
as it would sound impolite.
（4）あら
Mostly used by women, this is an exclamation of surprise, translatable as “oh my”, etc. Men can
use “え?” instead.
① A：あら、お父さん。今日は早いね。／Oh my, dear. You're home early
today.
B：そうなんだよ。／That's right.
source_file: 初级上/13.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第10课.md

title: Adjectives modifying nouns <attributive form of adjectives>
body_lines: Besides serving as predicates, adjectives can also be placed before nouns as modifiers — called the “attributive form
of the adjective” in Japanese grammar. As follows:
Type I adjectives: A + noun
Ⅰ
Type II adjectives: A + な + noun
Ⅱ
Type I adjectives can directly precede the noun they modify. Type II adjectives, when modifying a noun, need to be fol-
lowed by “な” before the noun. For this reason, some grammar books also call Type II adjectives “na-adjectives”, and
Type I adjectives ending in “い” “i-adjectives”.
① 白いパソコン／a white computer
② きれいな町／a clean, pretty town
source_file: 初级上/17.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第11课.md

title: N が <subject>
body_lines: Both particles “は” and “が” can mark the subject, but their usage differs slightly. Besides the
rules for using “は” and “が” mentioned earlier (Lesson 7, Grammar 3 and Lesson 9, Grammar 2),
within a stretch of context, when the subject is unknown (i.e. new to the listener) information, it must be marked with “が”.
Known, old information is marked with “は”. Compare:
① -1 ほら、あそこの 男 の人。あの人は中村さんのお兄さんですよ。／you
Look, that man over there. He is Nakamura's older brother.
① -2 由加：へえ、小学校の時の記念写真ですか。中村さんは、これ？／
Wow, is this a commemorative photo from elementary school? Nakamura, is this you?
中村：違いますよ。これがわたしです。／No. This is me.
In sentence ①-1, the “あの人” marked before the particle “は” is already known information
to the listener, so it is marked with “は”. The information the speaker wants to emphasize in this sentence is the part after “は”,
namely “中村さんのお兄さん”. In sentence ①-2, the “これ” that Nakamura points out
is unknown information to Yuka, and the sentence emphasizes the part marked by “が”, “こ
② こちらのパソコンが、今お得ですよ。／This computer here is a great deal right now.
③ A：日本語は難しいですか。／Is Japanese difficult?
B：ええ、文法が難しいです。／Yeah, the grammar is hard.
④ A：だれが留学生ですか。／Who is the international student?
B：あの人が留学生で、ジョージさんです。ジョージさんは今、先生の
研究室にいます。／He is the international student, George. He is now in the teacher's lab.
source_file: 初级上/17.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第11课.md

title: N と同じ
body_lines: “同じ” is a Type II adjective meaning “same; identical”. The particle “と” after a noun corre-
sponds to “with/and” in English. “〜と同じ” means “the same as ...”. When “同じ” modifies a noun,
the form “同じな” is not needed; “同じ” can modify the noun directly.
① 白いパソコンと同じ大きさです。／It's the same size as the white computer.
② 李さんは中村さんと同じ大学です。／Li goes to the same university as Nakamura.
③ 経済学部は法学部と同じ建物です。／The economics department and the law department are in the same building.
source_file: 初级上/17.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第11课.md

title: N がほしいです。
body_lines: “ほしい” is an adjective meaning “to want (to have something)”; its conjugation follows the Type I ad-
jective four quadrants (see Lesson 10, Grammar 2). The object wanted is generally marked with the particle “が”.
It corresponds to “(I) want ...”. Note that “ほしい” is generally
only used to express the first person's (the speaker's) desire for something, and is generally not used for the third person.
For the second person, it is mostly limited to close friends and family.
① （私は）新しいスーツケースがほしいです。／I want a new suitcase.
② 地下鉄がなかった時は、 車 がほしかったです。／Back when there was no subway,
I wanted a car.
“ほしい” can also modify a noun directly.
③ A：ほしいものはありますか。／Is there anything you want?
B：ありますよ。お金がほしいです。／Yes. I want money.
source_file: 初级上/17.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第11课.md

title: 句子 が、句子 。 ＜contrast＞
body_lines: The particle “が” connects two clauses and indicates a contrastive, adversative relation between them. “Sen-
tence が, sentence.” corresponds to “although ..., but ...” (as in the example
① 歴史の授業は難しいですが、面白いです。／History class is difficult but interesting.
When “が” follows “すみません” or “失礼です”, forming “すみませんが”,
“失礼ですが”, etc., its contrastive tone is weakened here and need not be translated into English.
Sometimes the following sentence is also omitted (as in example ③).
② 失礼ですが、お名前は？／Excuse me, what is your name?
③ 新しいパソコンがほしいのですが。／I'd like a new computer...
source_file: 初级上/17.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第11课.md

title: N も N も <(both)>
body_lines: The particle “も” used after each of two nouns forms “N も N も〜”, expressing parallelism.
It can be translated as “both N and N ...”.
① 兄も姉も会社員です。／Both my older brother and older sister are company employees.
② 日本料理も中華料理も美味しいです。／Both Japanese food and Chinese food are delicious.
④ メモリーもストレージも大きいです。／Both the memory and the storage are large.
source_file: 初级上/17.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第11课.md

title: Japanese “comparison” patterns
body_lines: There are many ways to express comparison in Japanese. Here we summarize the comparison patterns into the fol-
lowing forms:
（１）句型1 N は N より〜。
“より” is a case particle indicating the standard of comparison. This pattern says that N has more of the characteristic
shown by the predicate than N. Japanese “A はBより〜” is generally translated as “A is more ... than B”. When A has much more of the quality
explained in the predicate than B, Japanese often uses the adverb “ずっと”, translated as “much ...”.
① 中国は日本より広いです。／China is bigger than Japan.
② （こちらのパソコンは）さっきのよりメモリーがずっと大きいですよ。
／(This computer) has much more memory than the one from before.
③ スマホはパソコンより値段が高いです。／Smartphones are more expensive than computers.
（２）句型2 N より N のほうが〜。
This pattern is a variant of Pattern 1, meaning that compared with N, N has more of the characteristic
shown by the predicate. “ほう” can also be written “方”; it is a noun meaning “a certain side/direction”. “BよりA
のほうが〜” can be translated as “A is more ... than B”. Likewise, this pattern can also serve as the answer to Pattern 4
questions.
① 日本より中国のほうが広いです。／Compared with Japan, China is bigger.
② パソコンよりスマホのほうが値段が高いです。／Compared with computers, smartphones are
more expensive.
（３）句型3 N は N ほど〜（否定）。
The adverbial particle “ほど” follows a noun and indicates degree. When followed by a negative, this pattern says N does not have
the characteristic to the same degree as N. “Bは A ほど〜 (negative)” can be translated as “B is not as ... as A”,
“B doesn't ... as much as A”.
① 日本は中国ほど広くありません。／Japan is not as big as China.
② パソコンはスマホほど値段が高くありません。／Computers are not as expensive
as smartphones.
（４）句型4 N と N とどちら（のほう）が〜か。
This pattern is the question form of comparison sentences. It asks which of N and N has more of the characteristic
shown by the predicate. “A と B とどちら（のほう）が〜か” can be translated as “Which is (more) ..., A or B?”.
When choosing between the two, the answer usually uses the Pattern 2 form, with the “B より” part mostly omitted —
just answer “A のほうが〜”.
① A： 中国と日本とどちら（のほう）が広いですか。／Which is bigger, China or
Japan?
B：中国のほうが広いです。／China is bigger.
② A：パソコンとスマホとどちらが高いですか。／Which is more expensive, a computer or a smartphone?
B：スマホのほうが高いです。／The smartphone is more expensive.
source_file: 初级上/17.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第11课.md

title: –さ
body_lines: The suffix “−さ” can attach to the stem of Type I adjectives and some Type II adjectives to form a noun,
indicating degree or state. For example:
重い （[形Ⅰ]重的） → 重さ（[名]重量）
大きい（[形Ⅰ]大的） → 大きさ（[名]大小）
便利（[形Ⅱ] convenient） → 便利さ（[名] convenience; degree of convenience）
複雑 ([II-adj] complicated) → 複雑さ ([noun] complexity; degree of complexity)
① 重さはどれくらいですか。／How much does it weigh?
② 富士山の高さは何メートルですか。／How many meters high is Mt. Fuji?
③ パスワードは複雑さより長さのほうが大切です。／For passwords, length matters more
than complexity.
source_file: 初级上/17.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第11课.md

title: Polite spoken expressions in this lesson
body_lines: In many situations, Japanese people need to use

“polite language” (Japanese: “丁寧語”, often translated “courteous style”) when speaking to customers or people of higher status. This lesson covers several spoken expressions that become “polite language” just by swapping
specific words.
（１）では、こちらはいかがですか。
It means “Well then, how about this one?”. The conjunction “では” at the head of a sentence can be translated as “well then”,
and is often shortened to “じゃ” in spoken language.
“こちら” is the polite form of “これ”. “こちら” can also serve as the polite form of
“ここ”, referring to the speaker's location or things near the speaker. This substitution also applies to the other “こそ
あど” words.
“いかが” is the polite form of “どう”, also meaning “how; what about”. “こちらは
いかがですか” means basically the same as “これはどうですか”, but the former is more formal and
polite.
① A：もっと安いパソコンはありませんか。／Do you have a cheaper computer?
B：はい、こちらです。／Yes, this one.
②−1 来週はどうですか。／How about next week?
②−2 来週はいかがですか。／How about next week? (polite)
(2) こちらはどうでしょうか。 <でしょうか: polite form of ですか>
This sentence means basically the same as “こちらはいかがですか” above. Using “でしょう
か” instead of “ですか” makes the tone more indirect and courteous.
①−1 電話番号は何番ですか。／What is your phone number?
①−2 電話番号は何番でしょうか。／What is your phone number? (polite)
②−1だれですか。／Who is it?
②−2 どちら様でしょうか。／Who may I ask is calling? / Who are you? (polite)
source_file: 初级上/17.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第11课.md

title: N が〜 <object (case particle が−3)>
body_lines: Besides marking the subject, the particle “が” can also mark an object. In this lesson, “が”
marks the object of a certain ability or aptitude. Such ability-related words mainly consist of Type II adjectives (such as
“上手”, “下手”, “得意”, “苦手”, “好き”, “嫌い”) and verbs (such as “できます”, “わ
かります”).
Type II adjectives
上手／下手
好き／嫌い です。
N が とくい にがて
得意／苦手
Verbs
できます。
N が
わかります。
① 私は運動が嫌いです。／I don't like sports.
② 辛いものが苦手です。／I can't handle spicy food.
③ 兄は歴史が得意です。／My older brother is good at history.
④ 先生の話がよくわかりません。／I don't quite understand what the teacher says.
⑤ 父は料理ができます。／My father can cook.
source_file: 初级上/19.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第12课.md

title: （N の中で）N がいちばん〜 <particle “で”: scope>
body_lines: In Lesson 11 we learned several forms of Japanese comparison sentences. Here we learn the “superlative” form of adjective-predi-
cate sentences, expressing that within the scope shown by N, N has the most of the characteristic shown by the
predicate. The particle “で” after a noun delimits the scope; the adverb “いちばん” means “most”.
1 The “superlative” is an important point in English grammar: among three or more things or people, one has the most of some quality.
Here, the Japanese “superlative” corresponds to the “comparison” patterns of Lesson 11.
This pattern can be translated as “(among ...N...) N is the most ...”.
① 日本の漫画の中で、『スラムダンク』がいちばん好きです。／Among Japa-
nese manga, I like Slam Dunk the best.
② スポーツの中でバスケットボールがいちばん好きです。／sports; athletics
I like basketball the most.
③ クラスの中で、李さんがいちばん 頭 がいいです。／Li is the smart-
est in the class.
④ 日本料理の中で、お寿司がいちばん好きです。／Among Japanese dishes,
I like sushi the best.
source_file: 初级上/19.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第12课.md

title: N なので、〜 <cause-effect −2>
body_lines: The particle “ので” connects two clauses in a cause-effect relationship. In this pattern, when the first clause is a
“noun-predicate sentence” (see Lesson 5, Grammar 1), it can be joined directly in the form “N+な＋ので”;
this pattern can be translated as “because (it is) ...N..., ...”. Compared with “から”
from Lesson 9 (see Lesson 9, Grammar 4), “ので” tends to emphasize an objectively existing reason, and its tone
is more indirect and formal.
① 僕は神奈川県の湘南の出身なので、僕も『スラムダンク』が大good; fine
きですよ。／Because I'm from Shonan in Kanagawa Prefecture, I also love Slam Dunk
② 雨なので、運動会は中止です。／Because of rain, the sports day is cancelled.
③ 学生なので、お金がないです。／Because I'm a student, I have no money.
source_file: 初级上/19.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第12课.md

title: 〜は〜が、〜は〜。 <contrast (particle は–2)>
body_lines: In compound sentences expressing a contrastive relation, when the two clauses are similar in form and carry a sense of contrast,
the subjects of both clauses are marked with the particle “は”.
① バスケットボールはできませんが、サッカーとテニスはすこしでき
ます。／I can't play basketball, but I can play a little soccer and tennis.
② 日本語は 上手ですが、英語は下手です。／My Japanese is good, but my English is
poor.
③ 昨日は寒かったですが、今日はとても暑いです。／Yesterday was cold, but to-
day is very hot.
④ 私 は学生ですが、 妹 は会社員です。／I am a student, but my younger sister is a com-
pany employee.
source_file: 初级上/19.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第12课.md

title: N に〜 <object of a state or quality>
category: object of a state or quality
body_lines: The particle “に” follows a noun and indicates the object of the ability, attitude, quality, etc. that follows. After “に”
come mostly adjectives expressing quality, state, ability, etc.
① マスクは外出に必要です。／Masks are essential for going out.
② 横の 中国語訳は日本語学習 に便利です。／The Chinese translation beside it is convenient for learning
Japanese.
③ 兄は中国の歴史にも、日本の歴史にも詳しいです。／My brother knows both Chinese his-
tory and Japanese history well.
④ 駅の近くのアパートは、買い物に便利です。／The apartment near the station is convenient for
shopping.
source_file: 初级上/19.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第12课.md

title: 〜の（／ん）です。 <explanation −1 (adjectives, nouns)>
body_lines: Pattern: N + な + の（／ん）です。
A ＋の（／ん）です。
Ⅰ
A ＋な＋の（／ん）です。
Ⅱ
The pattern “〜の（／ん）です。” is very common in spoken Japanese; it can follow the “attributive form of an adjective”
or “noun + な”; in speech, the form “〜んです。” is mostly used. It expresses
a personal assertion, or an explanation of a situation. “〜の（／ん）です。” is hard to translate directly and is generally left untranslated. The specific functions and use
scenarios of the pattern “〜の（／ん）です。” are summarized below:
(1) Explaining a situation or giving a reason
Used to explain the “cause or reason” of what was stated before; mainly for the speaker's “explanation” of their situa-
tion. For example:
① 実は『キャプテン翼』も『テニスの王子様』も好きなんですよ。／Actually, I love both Captain
Tsubasa and The Prince of Tennis.
② すみません、今はちょっと 忙しいんです。／Sorry, I'm a bit busy right now.
③ 私は冷たい飲み物が苦手なんです。／I don't handle cold drinks well.
(2) Acceptance and realization
The situation described in the preceding text becomes the reason for the following “〜の（／ん）です”
sentence; the pattern “〜の（／ん）です” expresses the speaker's “acceptance” of that result,
with a sense of acknowledging and realizing the validity of one's own inference.
④ 由加さんは本当に漫画ファンなのですね。／Yuka, you really are a manga
fan.
(3) Stating the background of a topic, for indirect suggestions or requests
You can use “〜の（／ん）です” to state the background of a topic in order to make an indirect sug-
gestion or request. Here, “〜の（／ん）です” is mostly connected with the situation to be stated
afterward. This usage mostly appears in the form “〜の（／ん）ですが、〜”.
⑤ 新しいパソコンがほしいのですが。／I'd like to buy a new computer...
⑥ マックの最新モデルがいちばん軽いのですが。／The latest Mac model is the lightest...
right away.
⑦ あのう、テレビの音が大きいのですが。／Um, the TV is a bit loud...
Example ⑤ is a common expression when describing your specific needs to a shop assistant while shopping.
Example ⑥ uses the pattern “〜の（／ん）です” to explain to the other person, thereby imply-
ing “how about considering this one?”. Example ⑦ likewise indirectly explains the situation to express the speaker's implied request: could you turn the volume down?
source_file: 初级上/19.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第12课.md

title: Degree adverbs that can modify adjectives
body_lines: Degree adverbs that can modify adjectives include “超”, “とても”, “ちょっと”, “少し”, “あ
まり”, “全然”, etc. Among these, “超” has the highest degree and is mostly used in speech (example ①). In writing or
formal situations, “大変”, “非常に”, etc. can be used (example ②).
“ちょっと” and “少し” are similar in meaning, both indicating a small quantity of things or actions, a low
degree — like “a little; slightly”. “ちょっと” is used more in spoken language.
“あまり” must be followed by a negative form, meaning “(not) very ...” (example ③).
“全然” also needs to be followed by a negative form, translated as “(not) at all ...” (example ④). But in
modern Japanese society, “全然” can also be followed by an affirmative, with basically the same meaning as “とても” or “非常に”,
though this usage is generally not used in formal speech or business settings (example ⑤).
① 話のスピードが超速いです。／The speaking speed is super fast.
② 清華大学は 中 国で非常 に有名です。／Tsinghua University is very famous in China.
③ ここの家賃はあまり安くないです。／The rent here isn't very cheap.
④ イタリア語が全然わかりません。／I don't understand Italian at all.
⑤ A：忘年会、金曜日はどうですか？／How about Friday for the year-end party?
B：全然OK です。／Totally OK.
source_file: 初级上/19.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第12课.md

title: Other common spoken expressions in this lesson
body_lines: （１）じゃ、バスケットボールはお上手ですね。
Adding the prefix “お” before “上手” describes someone else being “good at something”. This
phrasing is more polite and is mostly used by women. Of course, “お上手” cannot be used about yourself.
（２）さすが由依さん。
The adverb “さすが” can be followed by a noun to emphasize that something fully matches one's prior expectation or judgment,
equivalent to “as expected of ...”, “truly worthy of ...”.
① さすが三つ星。料理がおいしくて美しい。サービスもいい。／As expected of three stars. The food is tasty and beautifully presented. The service is good too.
source_file: 初级上/19.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第12课.md

title: N (place) + へ（／に）+ movement V <movement>
body_lines: The particle “へ” follows a noun indicating a place and marks the direction of movement, used together with movement predi-
cate verbs (such as “行く”, “来る”, “帰る”). In this case “へ” is not read “he”
but “e”. The particle “へ” can also be replaced by “に”.
① 毎朝、会社へ行きます。／I go to the company every morning.
② いつ帰りますか。／When are you coming back?
③ 去年、家族と大阪に来ました。／I came to Osaka with my family last year.
source_file: 初级上/21.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第13课.md

title: Question word + も <total negation>
body_lines: A question word followed by the particle “も” and used with a negative predicate expresses total negation,
equivalent to “no ... at all”, “not any ...”.
① 夜中の博物館には誰もいません。／There is no one in the museum late at night.
② 引き出しには何もありません。／There is nothing in the drawer.
③ ここのカレー 料 理はどれもおいしくないです。／None of the curry dishes here are
any good.
④ この週末はどこにも行きません。／I'm not going anywhere this weekend.
source_file: 初级上/21.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第13课.md

title: Question word + か <indefinite>
body_lines: A question word followed by the particle “か” expresses indefiniteness. This usage is not limited to questions; it
can also be used in declarative sentences. Note that when “question word + か” is used in a question, it
forms a yes-no question, and the answer usually starts with “はい” or “いいえ”.
① あのレストランにお 客 さんが何人かいます。／There are a few customers
in that restaurant.
② 特に重要な理由がいくつかあります。／There are several particularly important reasons.
③ A：あのう、すみません。誰かいますか。／Excuse me, is anyone there?
B：はい。／Yes.
④ 以前、何回か来ました。／I've been here a few times before.
source_file: 初级上/21.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第13课.md

title: N から <starting point>
body_lines: The particle “から” can follow nouns indicating time, place, or order, marking the starting point of time, place,
or sequence — like “from ...” in English. “から” can also be followed directly by the copula
“です” to form a noun-predicate sentence.
① 体のトレーニングは明日からです。／Physical training starts tomorrow.
② 今から成績の発表です。／The announcement of grades starts now.
③ ここからはテストの内容です。／From here on is the content of the test.
The starting-point “から” can also be paired with the end-point particle “まで”.
④ 会議は今月の4日から6日までです。／The meeting is from the 4th to the 6th of this month.
source_file: 初级上/21.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第13课.md

title: Ｎじゃありませんか。
body_lines: This pattern is the rhetorical-question form of the noun-predicate sentence “Nです”. Equivalent to “isn't it ...?
”, with a tone of surprise or exclamation; mostly used in spoken language.
① とても有名な研究所じゃありませんか。／Isn't this a really famous research
institute!
② もう 1 2時50分じゃありませんか。／It's already 12:50!
③ あ、あの人は、鈴木さんじゃありませんか。／Ah, isn't that Suzuki over there?
source_file: 初级上/21.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第13课.md

title: けど <softened contrast, indirect tone>
body_lines: The conjunctive particle “けど” is the shortened form of “けれども” and expresses contrast. In this lesson, “けど”
is used at the end of a sentence for a softened contrast. This expression trails off, omitting the second half of the sentence; the tone is fairly
indirect and is mostly used in spoken language. Besides “けど”, “けれども” also has the forms “けれど” and “けど
① これから会議なんですけど。／We're about to have a meeting...
② そろそろお時間ですけれども。／It's about time...
③ A：中村さんはいますか。／Is Nakamura here?
B：はい、私ですけど。／Yes, that's me.
source_file: 初级上/21.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第13课.md

title: The plain forms of nouns and adjectives, and their use in plain-style conversation
body_lines: (1) Plain forms of noun-predicate sentences and adjective-predicate sentences
Japanese mainly has two speech styles: “polite” and “plain”. The plain style, as opposed to the polite style, is mostly used in conversations between friends
or family, or in written forms such as novels and papers. When using Japanese, you need to choose the appropriate
style according to the relationship between the two parties.
Taking the noun 学生 as an example, the four-quadrant comparison table of polite and plain noun-predicate sentences is summarized in Table 13-1.
Table 13-1: Four-quadrant comparison of polite and plain noun-predicate sentences (example: 学生)
Tense | Style | Affirmative | Negative
学生ではありません。
Present/ | Polite | 学生です。 | がくせい
Or: 学生ではないです。
Future
Plain | 学生だ。 | 学生ではない。
学生ではありませんでした。
Polite | 学生でした。
Past | Or: 学生ではなかったです。
Plain | 学生だった。 | 学生ではなかった。
(In spoken language, “では” can be replaced by “じゃ”)
The comparison table of polite and plain adjective-predicate sentences is summarized in Table 13-2.
Table 13-2: Four-quadrant comparison of polite and plain adjective-predicate sentences
Adjective
Tense | Style | Affirmative | Negative
type
高くありません。
Present/ | Polite | 高いです。 | たか
或：高くないです。
Type I | Future
adjective | Plain | 高い。 | 高くない。
高くありませんでした。
たか | Polite | 高 たか かったです。
（高い） たか
Past | Or: 高くなかったです。
Plain | 高かった。 | 高くなかった。
静かではありません。
Present/ | Polite | 静かです。 | しず
Or: 静かではないです。
Type II | Future
adjective | Plain | 静かだ。 | 静かではない。
静かではありませんでした。
（ し 静 ず か） | Polite | 静 しず かでした。 | しず
Past | Or: 静かではなかったです。
Plain | 静かだった。 | 静かではなかった。
(In spoken language, “では” can be replaced by “じゃ”)
(2) Switching between polite and plain styles in speech
The speech style in spoken Japanese changes according to the listener, the situation, and the topic. One such situa-
tion is that even in a mainly polite-style conversation, the plain style can be used when the speaker voices their own feelings (such as surprise or emer-
gency). The “本当だ！”, “やばい！”
and “じゃ、図書館だ！” in this lesson's model dialogue are Nakamura's self-talk when feeling surprised or flustered, and therefore
use the plain form.
① このたこ焼き、おいしいね。／This takoyaki is tasty.
② 火事だ！／Fire!
③ ハチ君、かわいい！／Hachi is so cute!
source_file: 初级上/21.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第13课.md

title: Other common spoken expressions in this lesson
body_lines: （１）お借りします。
When borrowing something from someone, Japanese people generally use this phrase as a courtesy. It is a polite expression,
meaning “let me borrow this”.
① A：そこの自転車、お借りしますね。／That bicycle — I'll borrow it, okay?
B：はーい。／Sure.
（２）行ってきます。
Japanese people have set greetings for leaving and returning. When about to leave (home, the office, etc.),
they say “行ってきます。”, meaning “I'm off”, “I'll be back”. The people staying behind
reply “行ってらっしゃい”, equivalent to “take care; see you later”.
In addition, upon returning they say “ただいま。 (I'm home)”, and the people at home (or in the office)
respond with “お帰りなさい。” (welcome back).
① (about to leave) 息子：行ってきます。／I'm off.
母：行ってらっしゃい。／See you later.
② (coming back in) 息子：ただいま。／I'm home.
母：お帰りなさい。／Welcome home.
source_file: 初级上/21.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第13课.md

title: Conjugation classes of verbs
body_lines: Classifying verbs by their conjugation type is the first step to efficiently mastering verb sentences. Traditional Japanese
school grammar and the more recently popular Japanese textbooks classify verb conjugations slightly differently, but mostly
they differ only in the names of the types. Here we summarize the conjugation types of Japanese verbs with their Japanese names, morphological features,
and example words in Table 14-1. The “dictionary form” of a verb is also called the “basic form” or “plain
form” — the original form in which a verb appears as a dictionary entry, without any conjugation.
Table 14-1: List of Japanese verb conjugation types
Verb class | Japanese name | Morphological features | Examples
休む、願う、
Type I verbs | 五段動詞 | The dictionary form ends in a u-row kana
わかる、ある
The dictionary form ends in “る”, preceded by 寝る、起きる、
Type II verbs | 一段動詞 |
an i-row or e-row kana | 忘れる
Can be “する” (used alone). する、勉 強 する、
サ変動詞
Type III verbs | Can also be formed by “Sino-Japanese word + する”. 運動する、運転する
カ変動詞 | Only the single verb “来る” 来る
source_file: 初级上/23.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第14课.md

title: The polite form of verbs and the masu-stem <V ます形>
body_lines: When Japanese verbs are used, the polite suffix “ます” is added after the dictionary form.
When the verb takes the suffix “ます”, the verb's form changes according to its conjugation class;
this change is called “verb conjugation”.
The specific rules for the change before “ます” are as follows:
Group I (godan) verbs:
Change the final u-row kana of the verb to the corresponding i-row kana, then attach “ます”. For example:
休む：やすむ→み＋ます＝休みます
願う：ねがう→い＋ます＝願います
ある：ある→り＋ます＝あります
Group II (ichidan) verbs:
Remove the final kana “る” of the verb, then attach “ます”. For example:
起きる：おきる＋ます＝起きます
寝る：ねる＋ます＝寝ます
忘れる：忘れる＋ます＝忘れます
Group III (irregular) verbs:
① Suru-verbs: “する”. Change “する” to “し”, then attach “ます”. That is:
する：する→し＋ます＝します
勉強する：勉強する→し＋ます＝勉強します
② Kuru-verb: “来る”. Change “来る” to “来”, then attach “ます”. That is:
来る：来る→き＋ます＝来ます
In addition, the verb stem that remains after removing “ます” is called the
“masu-stem of the verb”, marked in this book's grammar notes as “V ます形” (in Japanese school grammar also called “動
詞（第一）連用形”). For example, the dictionary form of “ある” is “ある”. In use, the polite form of “あ
る” is “あります”; “あり” is the “masu-stem” of “あります”. For ease of
understanding, examples are given in Table 14-2.
Table 14-2: List of dictionary forms, polite forms, and ren'yokei (masu-stems)
Verb class | Dictionary form | Polite form | Ren'yokei (masu-stem)
Type I verbs | わかる | わかります | わかり
Type II verbs | 忘れる | 忘れます | 忘れ
Type III verbs
来る | 来ます | 来
source_file: 初级上/23.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第14课.md

title: N (time) に <point in time>
body_lines: The particle “に” follows a time noun and marks the point in time at which an action occurs.
① 日曜日の午後１時半に会いましょうか。／Let's meet at 1:30 pm on Sunday.
② いつも夜9時に寝ます。／I always go to bed at 9 pm.
③ 1 3日に中村さんの誕生日パーティーがあります。／On the 13th, there's Nakamura's birthday party.
mura's birthday party.
source_file: 初级上/23.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第14课.md

title: Time + ごろ
body_lines: The suffix “ごろ” after a specific time noun expresses an approximate time, translatable as “about;
around”. “ごろ” can also be written “頃”. When a time noun is followed by “ごろ”, the particle
“に” marking the point in time can be omitted.
① いつも夜 1 1時ごろ寝ます。／I always sleep around 11 pm.
② 今日は2時ごろに帰ります。／I'm going home around 2 today.
③ 3月ごろ、桜が咲きます。／The cherry blossoms bloom around March.
④ 2000年ごろから、車が多くなりました。／From around 2000, cars
increased.
source_file: 初级上/23.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第14课.md

title: 〜くらい（ぐらい）
body_lines: In Japanese, “〜くらい（ぐらい）” can follow quantity words for time, money, count, etc.,
expressing an approximate number — like “about; around” in English.
① 発表は全部で２時間ぐらいでした。／The presentation was about two hours in total.
② 食費は毎月３万円ぐらいです。／Food expenses are about 30,000 yen a month.
③ 教室には学生が5人ぐらいいます。／There are about 5 students in the classroom.
source_file: 初级上/23.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第14课.md

title: なる <change>
body_lines: Pattern: N + に + なる
A （い）→く＋なる
Ⅰ
A ＋に＋なる
Ⅱ
“なる” is one of the verbs that best embodies the characteristics of Japanese, used to describe the natural change of things, or of their qual-
ities and states. “なる” can be combined with nouns, adjectives, verbs, and other parts of speech.
This lesson mainly covers the use of “なる” with nouns and adjectives. The specific joining rules are as follows:
Noun: N + に + なる Example: 会社員 → 会社員になる
Type I adjective: A（い）→ く + なる Example: 寒い → 寒くなる
Ⅰ
Type II adjective: A + に + なる Example: 静か → 静かになる
Ⅱ
① 1 1月の初めから寒くなります。／It gets cold from the beginning of November.
② 体調が大分よくなりました。／My physical condition has improved a lot.
③ 日本語がかなり上手になりました。／My Japanese has become quite good.
④ 今週末のイベントは 中止になりました。／This weekend's event has been cancelled.
⑤ でも、午後から眠くなるから、何もできなくなります。／But from the afternoon on I get sleepy,
so I can't do anything.
Example ⑤ “何もできなくなります” means “(become) unable to do anything”. The
“できない” in the sentence is the negative form of the verb “できる (can; to be able to)” (covered in detail in Lesson
17). When “できない” is followed by the verb “なる”, the negative “ない” changes to
“なく” before “なる” to express change.
source_file: 初级上/23.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第14课.md

title: V ましょう。／V ましょうか。 <invitation (V ましょう−1)>
body_lines: Lesson 10's “Expression Expansion” 3 briefly introduced the use of the “（いっしょに）Nをしましょう
か” pattern and how to respond. Here we explain the use of “V ましょう。/V ましょうか。” in de-
tail. “ましょう” after the masu-stem of a verb expresses an invitation, suggesting that the other person do something together with you.
It is often paired with the adverb “いっしょに”, equivalent to “let's ... (together)”.
Adding the interrogative particle “か” after “V ましょう” softens the tone further,
with the feel of asking for the other person's consent.
① そろそろ帰りましょう。／Let's head back soon.
② A：昼休みは、あそこの店へ行きましょうか。／Shall we go to that shop for lunch break?
from now on.
B：そうしましょう。／Let's do that.
③ A：今晩、家でゲームしましょうか。／Shall we play games at my place tonight?
B：いいですね。／Sounds good.
source_file: 初级上/23.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第14课.md

title: 〜ほうがいい <suggestion −1 (nouns, adjectives)>
body_lines: Pattern: N + の + ほうがいい
A attributive form (i.e. A) + ほうがいい
Ⅰ Ⅰ
A attributive form (i.e. A + な) + ほうがいい
Ⅱ Ⅱ
The noun “ほう” means “(a certain) side/direction”; the pattern of “noun + の” or the attributive form of an adjective followed by “ほうが
いい” is used when the speaker gives advice to the listener, translated as “it's better to ...”, “... is better”.
① もっと効率的なもののほうがいいですよ。／A more efficient way is better.
② 新 しいアパートは会社に近いほうがいいです。／It's better for the new apartment to be
close to the company.
③ 毎日の 食材は安全なほうがいいです。／For everyday ingredients, safer is better.
books.
source_file: 初级上/23.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第14课.md

title: Talking about durations of time
body_lines: (1) Hours
In Japanese, “... hours” is expressed with “〜時間”, and “... and a half hours” with “〜
時間半”. See Table 14-1 for details.

(2) Minutes

title: Japanese transitive/intransitive verbs and the particle “を” <“を”: marking the object>
body_lines: Japanese verbs can be divided into intransitive and transitive verbs. Intransitive verbs cannot take an object, much like
“intransitive verbs” in English. Transitive verbs can take an object, much like the English “transitive verb” concept. Of
course, some individual Japanese verbs have both intransitive and transitive properties.
When using a transitive verb, the particle “を” is placed after the noun to mark the object of the verb.
① 本を読みます。／I read a book.
② 資料を調べます。／I look up materials.
When the object part becomes the topic, the particle “は” or “も” can replace “を”.
③ メールはよく送りますが、手紙はあまり書きません。／I often send emails, but I don't write letters much.
④ 休みの日は、よく映画を見ます。買い物もします。／On days off I often watch
movies. I also go shopping.
source_file: 初级上/25.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第15课.md

title: N で
body_lines: (1) “で” marks <place>
The particle “で” follows a noun indicating a place or location, marking the place where an action takes place, translatable
as “at; in”.
① 伊藤先生のゼミでデータを集めました。／I collected data in Professor Ito's semi-
nar.
② 私はよく喫茶店で小説を読みます。／I often read novels in cafés.
③ 日本では、口頭試験はどんな 準備をしますか。／In Japan, how do you prepare for an
oral exam?
(2) “で” marks <tool, means>
The particle “で” follows a noun and indicates the tool or means used to perform an action, gener-
ally translated as “with; by; using ...”.
① スマホで外国語を勉強します。／I study foreign languages on my smartphone.
② インターネットで資料を調べます。／I look up materials on the internet.
③ 日本人はお箸で料理を食べます。／Japanese people eat with chopsticks.
(3) “で” marks <cause, reason>
The particle “で” after a noun can also indicate a cause or reason, translated as “because of ...”.
① 中村さんは毎日、試験勉強 で大変なんですよ。／Nakamura has a hard time every day be-
cause of exam preparation.
② 病気で学校を休みました。／I was absent from school because of illness.
③ 地震で電車が止まりました。／The trains stopped because of the earthquake.
source_file: 初级上/25.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第15课.md

title: N に <object of an action>
body_lines: The particle “に” follows a noun and marks the target of the following action.
① 中村さんにメールで資料を送ります。／I send materials to Nakamura by email.
② 午後、ジョージさんに会います。／I'm meeting George in the afternoon.
③ 友達に簡単なやり方を聞きます。／I ask a friend for an easy way to do it.
source_file: 初级上/25.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第15课.md

title: N なら
body_lines: “なら” is also called a “topic-highlighting particle”; attached to a noun, it highlights that noun as the topic.
So what kind of nouns can be highlighted by “なら”? Generally, something the other
person just said, a topic discussed before, or something predictable from the context can all be
brought up as the topic. The “英語なら” in this lesson's dialogue belongs to the first case. “N なら、〜” corre-
sponds to “if it's ... (N), then ...” in English.
① 日本語の小説なら、家には何冊かありますよ。／Speaking of Japanese novels,
I have several at home.
② A：新しいパソコンがほしいんですが。／I'd like a new computer...
B：パソコンなら、こちらがいいですよ。／If it's computers, this one is good.
③ A：一緒に喫茶店に行きましょうか。／Shall we go to a café together?
B：コーヒーなら、スタバのがいいですね。／If it's coffee, Starbucks is
good.
source_file: 初级上/25.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第15课.md

title: N について
body_lines: “について” follows a noun and is used to bring up a topic, translated as “about; regarding”. “について”
can be followed by “です” to form a predicate sentence, or by a predicate sentence with a verb.
① 経済のグローバリゼーションについてです。／It's about economic globalization.
② 先週 の旅行について作文を書きました。／I wrote an essay about last week's
trip.
③ 今日の授業 について、何か質問はありますか。／Do you have any questions about today's
lesson?
source_file: 初级上/25.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第15课.md

title: About offering help
body_lines: When you want to proactively offer help or do something for someone, you can use the following two ways to
express it.
(1) V ましょう／V ましょうか <volition, suggestion (V ましょう–2)>
In Lesson 14 we already learned the invitational use of “V ましょう”, i.e. suggesting that oth-
ers do something together with you. Besides invitation, “V ましょう” can also be used to proactively offer help
to someone, expressing the speaker's offer to perform an action themselves.
“か” carries a questioning tone; “V ましょうか” has the feel of seeking the other person's consent and is softer than
“V ましょう”. When using this pattern, the subject is mostly first person (usually omit-
ted), and the beneficiary of the action is mostly the listener.
① A：手伝いましょうか。／Shall I help you?
B：すみません。お願いします。／Sorry to trouble you. Please do.
② A：荷物を持ちましょうか。／Shall I carry your luggage?
B：大丈夫です。ありがとうございます。／I'm fine. Thank you.
③ メールでは時間がかかりますから、電話をかけましょうか。／Email
takes too long, so let me give them a call.
（２）僕も協 力しますよ。
Besides “V ましょう／V ましょうか”, you can also use “協力します。” to more di-
rectly express your willingness to help. Note that when the first person does a favor for the second person,
or does something for them, there is no need to specifically point out for whom it is done. So just using the verb 「協
力します」 expresses “I'll help (you)”.
① A：明日、本番なんです。もう、準備が間に合いません。／The performance is tomorrow. We won't be ready in time.
B：そうですか。協 力しますよ。／I see. I'll help you.
source_file: 初级上/25.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第15课.md

title: How to respond when someone offers help
body_lines: （１）to accept; to receive
When you are willing to accept the help offered, you can use the following sentences.
① A：それ、持ちましょうか。／Shall I carry that for you?
B：助かります。ありがとうございます。／That's a great help. Thank you.
② A：それ、持ちましょうか。／Shall I carry that for you?
B：すみません。お願いします。／Sorry to trouble you. Please do.
The “助かります。” in example ① means “to be helped; to be saved”. When someone offers
to help, you can use “助かります。” to express gratitude.
The “お願いします” in example ② is a polite expression you can use when asking someone to do something for you,
translated as “please; I'm counting on you”.
（２）refusal; rejection
If you need to decline the other person's kind offer, you can first thank them and then use the following sentence.
① A：それ、持ちましょうか。／Shall I carry that for you?
B：あ、大丈夫です。ありがとうございます。／Ah, I'm fine. Thank you.
source_file: 初级上/25.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第15课.md

title: Describing the sequence of actions or situations
body_lines: You can place conjunctions such as “まず”, “それから”, “そして”, “その後”, and “最後に” at the
head of sentences to describe the sequence of actions or situations. These words mean “first”, “then”, “moreover”,
and “finally” respectively.
① まず、自分でテーマを考えます。／First, think of a topic yourself.
② それから、原稿を書きます。／Then, write the script.
③ そして、辞書で単語の読み方を調べます。／Also, look up the readings of words in a dictionary.
④ 最後に、たくさん練習します。／Finally, practice a lot.
source_file: 初级上/25.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第15课.md

title: V masu-stem + に + 行く/来る/帰る <purposeful movement>
body_lines: The particle "に" follows the verb masu-stem or an action noun (for suru-verbs, just the stem)
and is followed by a movement verb to express the purpose of the movement. Can be translated as "go (to a place) to ..."
do ... (an action)".
① 教室に忘れ物を取りに行きます。／Go to the classroom to pick up something left behind.
② サークルの仲間たちとお花見に行きます。／Go cherry-blossom viewing with my club friends.
③ 昨日中村さんのお家に遊びに行きました。／Yesterday I went to Nakamura's place to hang out.
④ 散歩に出かけましょうか。／Shall we go out for a walk?
⑤ 資料を届けに来ました。／(I) came to deliver the materials.
source_file: 初级上/27.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第16课.md

title: V ます形＋ながら、〜
body_lines: "ながら" follows the verb masu-stem and indicates that two actions happen simultaneously or keep alternating,
equivalent to "... while ..." in English.
① 考えながら、パワーポイントを作ります。／Make PowerPoint slides while thinking.
② 弟 はいつも音楽を聴きながら、宿題をします。／My little brother always listens to mu-
sic while doing homework.
③ お茶をしながら、話しましょうか。／Shall we chat over tea?
source_file: 初级上/27.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第16课.md

title: Quantifier + も <subjectively many>
body_lines: A quantifier followed by the particle "も" shows the speaker subjectively considers the amount large. In example ①, un-
der normal circumstances three students is not many, but when the speaker feels three students is a lot,
"も" can be added after the quantifier "3人" to convey the speaker's subjective sense that the number
is large.
① 教室に学生が3人もいます。／There are (as many as) three students in the classroom.
② 議論は3日も続きました。／The discussion lasted (a whole) three days.
③ 日系企業を５社も訪問しました。／(We) visited (as many as) five Japanese companies.
The "何冊" appearing in this lesson's dialogue, although an interrogative word, is also a quantifier. When the inter-
rogative quantifier "何冊" is followed by the particle "も", even though the number is indefinite, it carries the sense
of subjectively regarding it as many; it is not a question.
④ あの映画は何度も見ましたよ。／I've seen that movie many times.
source_file: 初级上/27.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第16课.md

title: 〜でしょ（う） <confirmation, rhetorical question I>
body_lines: Pattern: noun + でしょ（う）
adjective + でしょ（う）
"でしょ（う）" is read with rising intonation and is mostly used for confirmation, with a rhetorical tone; in speech the "でし"
ょ" form is more common. Can be translated as "... right?"
① 李さんも留学生でしょ？／Li is an international student too, right?
② 勉強のほうが大事でしょう？／Studying is more important, isn't it?
③ タバコを止めましょうよ。体に悪いでしょう？／Let's quit smoking. It's bad for your
health, you know?
source_file: 初级上/27.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第16课.md

title: ため ＜purpose＞
body_lines: The formal noun "ため" expresses purpose and can be translated as "for the sake of". When followed by a noun, connect it with the particle "の".
When the purpose is a noun, use the form "Nのため". "そのための本" can be translated as "a book for
that purpose".
① ここは小学生のための教室です。／This is a classroom for elementary school students.
② 海外旅行のためのタオルを買いました。／(I) bought a towel for the overseas trip.
③ 期末試験のための勉強計画を 考 えます。／Think up a study plan for preparing for the final
exam.
source_file: 初级上/27.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第16课.md

title: 〜の（／ん）です。 <explanation II (verbs)>
body_lines: Pattern: verb plain form + の（／ん）です。
In Lesson 12 we learned the form of "〜の（／ん）です。" following nouns and adjectives,
used to explain a situation. This lesson covers the form with the verb plain form followed by "〜の（／ん）で
Besides the three specific usage scenarios and functions learned in Lesson 12, "〜の（／ん）です" can also
be used in questions to ask the listener to explain the question raised. In this case, the preceding context usually
contains a premise or background for the question, or the speaker, after making a subjective judgment about a situation,
seeks an explanation from the listener. For example:
① A：一緒に本屋へ行きませんか。／Won't you come to the bookstore with me?
B：本屋へ何をしに行くんですか。／What are you going to the bookstore for?
② A：もう帰るんですか。／Are you going home already?
B：ええ、もう時間なので。／Yes, it's late.
③ A：お腹が痛いんですか。／Does your stomach hurt?
B：ええ、ちょっと。／Yes, a little.
source_file: 初级上/27.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第16课.md

title: V ませんか。 <invitation>
body_lines: This expression is used when the speaker suggests or invites someone to do something (together); its tone is softer than "V ましょ
うか". It can also be paired with the adverb "いっしょに". Can be translated as "(won't you ...)
(together)?"
① 来週のサークル活動にいっしょに参加しませんか。／Won't you join next week's club activity
with me?
② 明日、映画を見に行きませんか。／Want to go see a movie tomorrow?
③ ここで写真を撮りませんか。／Shall we take a photo here?
source_file: 初级上/27.梁爽老师日语精讲精练：第16课.md

title: Other common spoken expressions in this lesson
body_lines: The sentence-final particle "よね" is composed of "よ" and "ね", so it carries the nuances of both "よ" and "ね".
When the speaker is fairly confident about their statement or judgment but still wants to confirm with the listener,
"よね" can be used.
① A：そのための本は、ありませんよね。／The book for that purpose — you don't have it,
right?
B：うん、ありません。じゃ、買いに行きましょう。／No, I don't. Well then,
let's go buy it.
② A：日本では富士山がいちばん高いですよね。／In Japan, Mt. Fuji is the highest, right?
B：そうですね。／That's right.
③ A：３限の講義の 教室は3 0 1 教室ですよね。／The 3rd-period lecture's classroom is
301, right?
B：違いますよ。 3 02です。／No, it's 302.
The conjunction "実は" is placed at the beginning of a sentence to add further information to what was just men-
tioned, or to tell the listener the actual facts. Generally, what follows "実は" is something the listener mostly
doesn't know.
① A：昨日は授業で何をしましたか。／What did you do in class yesterday?
B：実は、授業には行きませんでした。／Actually, I didn't go to class.
② A：これ、食べませんか。／Won't you eat this?
B：実は、鶏肉が苦手なんです。／Actually, I'm not good with chicken.
（３）ところで、〜
